overview.title: Overview
overview.content: An earthquake is a sudden slip on a fault line that releases radiated seismic energy and causes ground shaking; it can also be triggered by volcanic or magmatic activity or other sudden stress changes in the earth. Most earthquakes last a minute or less, but aftershocks can continue for days, weeks or months depending on magnitude. Size is most commonly measured using the Moment Magnitude scale (Mw), a logarithmic measure where each one-unit increase corresponds to roughly 32 times more energy release, and each two-unit increase to about 1000 times more energy; earthquakes of 7.0 or above can cause intense shaking and serious consequences over a wide area, while those of 6.0–6.9 may cause heavy damage in populated areas and smaller events can still damage weak structures near the epicentre. Shaking severity is also described qualitatively with the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale (I to XII, with structural damage typically starting around VI) and quantified with ground motion parameters such as peak ground acceleration (PGA), peak ground velocity (PGV) and spectral acceleration (SA). Overall impact is mainly determined by the intensity of ground shaking combined with the quality of structural engineering and building codes in the region, with soil conditions, emergency service preparedness and community resilience as additional contributing factors.

hazards.title: Primary and secondary hazards
hazards.content: The primary hazards of an earthquake are ground shaking, surface fault rupture and fissures, and subsidence or uplift; the strength and duration of shaking at a given location depend on magnitude, distance to the epicentre, depth, and local soil conditions, with deeper earthquakes generally producing lower surface intensity than shallow ones of the same magnitude. Secondary hazards include landslides and debris flows (especially in mountainous areas), liquefaction of saturated sandy sediments that can cause structures to sink, tsunamis generated by earthquakes near coasts, and seiche-like waves affecting areas near large bodies of water; earthquakes can also change river courses and cause flash floods. Fires are a common secondary effect, often triggered by downed power lines or ruptured gas lines, and can be worsened if water lines are also broken, leaving insufficient water for firefighting. Dams, embankments and levees may fail during an earthquake, causing downstream flooding; damage to infrastructure can also release hazardous materials, contributing to Natech events (natural hazard triggering technological disasters) such as industrial accidents. Aftershocks following the main event reset the hazard picture and can cause further collapse of already-damaged buildings.

physical.title: Physical impact
physical.content: The degree of building damage depends on structural and horizontal/vertical irregularities, the frequency content of the shaking, soil conditions, and the inherent resilience of the structure; poorly designed, inspected or constructed buildings, particularly unreinforced masonry, are most likely to fail and collapse. Buildings that are only slightly or moderately damaged in the main shock may collapse during large aftershocks. Earthquakes can severely damage infrastructure and lifelines, including power cables, telecommunications, water and sanitation pipes, and gas lines, which can be ruptured or severed, hampering both relief efforts and daily life. Access can be further compromised by destruction of roads, bridges, ports and airports, and by landslides or debris blocking routes. In recent large events, hundreds of thousands of buildings have been severely damaged or collapsed and critical energy infrastructure has sustained damage, illustrating the scale possible in major earthquakes.

people.title: Impact on people
people.content: Trauma from building collapse or other seismic activity is the leading cause of death, accounting for up to 75-80% of fatalities, while death is rare for people outdoors at the time of the earthquake. Structural collapses generate trapped victims who may survive for days under favourable conditions, but 85-95% of people rescued alive from collapsed buildings are found within the first 24-48 hours, making the early hours and days critical for search and rescue. Most injured individuals, mainly minor cuts, bruises and fractures with a smaller share of severe multi-trauma and crush syndrome cases, arrive at medical facilities within three to five days, often in two waves (local casualties first, then referred cases from further afield as relief is organised), with victims of secondary hazards such as aftershocks and fires arriving later. Disease outbreaks in the weeks following an earthquake are possible but usually of modest proportions. Earthquakes can have long-lasting mental health effects, particularly PTSD among children and teenagers, and while households typically begin recovery immediately, major population displacement can occur in heavily damaged urban areas.

aggravating.title: Aggravating factors
aggravating.content: Proximity to the epicentre and shallow depth both increase shaking intensity and the extent of damage. The time of day affects severity, since nighttime events can trap more people asleep in vulnerable buildings and can hinder emergency mobilisation. Poorly designed, inspected and constructed buildings, especially unreinforced or weak masonry, and high population density both increase losses, as do local soil conditions that amplify shaking. Lack of earthquake awareness or warning systems increases risk-taking behaviours that raise vulnerability. Cold-climate winter events raise risks of hypothermia and frostbite for survivors and can hinder rescue, while indoor stoves and fires during cold weather increase post-earthquake fire risk; conversely, hot climates and water scarcity reduce survival chances for people trapped in rubble. Hospitals may also suffer power outages risking intensive care patients, and staff may leave their posts to check on relatives.

assessment.title: Monitoring, rapid assessment and post-event investigation
assessment.content: Earthquakes cannot currently be predicted in location, magnitude or time, though Earthquake Early Warning systems using seismic sensor networks can give up to several seconds of notice, mainly used to automatically shut down critical infrastructure, and tsunami warning centres use detected earthquake parameters to assess tsunamigenic potential and issue coastal warnings. Within about 30 minutes of an event, systems such as GDACS automatically generate an alert level with event maps, shakemaps, exposure and estimated casualties, and satellite mapping services (e.g. Copernicus Emergency Management Service) can subsequently be activated to assess building and road damage from remote sensing. Following significant earthquakes, structured post-event investigations are organised in phases: activation within minutes to days, perishable-data reconnaissance (geoscience, engineering and social science data collection) over days to months, and research/knowledge transfer over months to years, producing products such as event pages (within a day), priorities workshops (1-3 months), event summaries and after-action reports (3 months-1 year), and in-depth integrative publications after 2-5+ years. Field missions, such as those conducted by JRC ELSA after Molise and L'Aquila earthquakes, and rapid dam-breach scenario modelling, are examples of this reconnaissance process, which also feeds National Seismic Risk Assessments.

needs.title: Typical needs
needs.content: Urban search and rescue (USAR) teams, ideally INSARAG-certified, are needed urgently to locate and extract trapped survivors, since speed is critical. Medical care needs include temporary field hospitals with emergency personnel and supplies as local facilities become overwhelmed. Logistics needs cover congested air and overland transport, damaged roads, ports, bridges and disrupted supply chains, requiring temporary solutions to move aid and evacuate people. Emergency shelter and non-food items (tents, cots, blankets) are needed as people avoid damaged homes due to aftershock risk, alongside food, water, sanitation (latrines, hygiene items), restoration of power (generators, repair crews), communication networks (temporary cell towers, satellite phones), and heavy equipment for debris removal to clear access and support search and rescue.

response.title: Response and coordination
response.content: Effective response requires coordination across government agencies, disaster relief organisations, businesses, community groups and civil society, often including UNDAC teams and international USAR teams deployed from multiple countries, as seen with the 23 USAR teams from 9 countries and 18 UNDAC members deployed in a documented example. Mechanisms such as the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM) can be activated to provide expertise and in-kind items, supported by ERCC Liaison Officers and Union Civil Protection Teams assisting UNDAC coordination. Scientific and humanitarian stakeholders collaborate to support response, including exchanging damage, fatality and injury estimates, hydrometeorological forecasts, and rapid hazard modelling (e.g., dam breach scenarios) to inform operational decisions. Response actions must avoid interfering with ongoing technical investigation efforts, and coordination calls and technical clearinghouses help organisations and field teams share plans and data in real time.

risk_reduction.title: Risk reduction
risk_reduction.content: Earthquakes cannot be prevented, but related vulnerability, exposure and risk can be reduced through seismic retrofitting, enforcement of modern design codes (such as Eurocode 8), strategic urban planning that avoids construction on soft soils, cliff faces or active faults, and risk awareness campaigns. Probabilistic and scenario-based seismic risk assessments (using tools such as OpenQuake, SELENA, HAZUS, ELER) inform national risk assessments and the prioritisation of retrofitting and funding; for example, Italy allocated about EUR 1 billion to a national seismic prevention programme distributed according to assessed risk. Studies combining seismic risk with energy efficiency and socioeconomic vulnerability have identified 100 priority EU regions for renovation, where renovating cost-beneficial building classes could reduce annual fatalities by 28-36% and achieve tens of millions of euros in annual economic loss reduction. Research infrastructures (e.g., European Laboratory for Structural Assessment, reaction wall and shake-table testing of frames, slabs, viaducts and base isolation systems) support development of more resilient construction, retrofitting techniques and removable structural components.

recovery.title: Recovery and lessons
recovery.content: Households typically begin recovery efforts immediately after an earthquake, and major population displacement, while rare, can occur in heavily damaged urban areas. The post-earthquake investigation process is designed to feed directly into recovery and future mitigation: documented lessons on damage and disruption, including cases of good structural performance, are synthesised over 2-5+ years into reports intended to reduce losses in future events through improved planning, design and construction practices, and long-term studies can continue for years to decades to capture the full socioeconomic and recovery trajectory. Seismic risk mitigation is also framed as a sound financial investment, reducing property loss, deaths, disruption of services and the costs of sheltering and search and rescue, and integrated renovation (structural plus energy efficiency) is highlighted as an opportunity to build back better while contributing to economic recovery and climate goals.

nodes.label: Primary earthquake hazards
nodes.description: Direct earthquake phenomena including ground shaking, surface fault rupture, fissures, subsidence and uplift.

includes.label: Ground shaking
includes.description: Sudden slip on a fault produces radiated seismic energy that results in ground shaking; strength and duration depend on magnitude, distance to epicentre and local soil conditions. Ground shaking is described as the most damaging effect of earthquakes, affecting built and natural environments and triggering other hazards.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Surface fault rupture and fissures
includes.description: Sudden slip on a fault can cause surface rupture and fissures. Example: a raised ground 'mole track' along a fault rupture during the M7.1 Ridgecrest earthquake crossing a dry lake bed; a fault offset of about 5 m near the Denali Fault earthquake. In the Türkiye earthquakes, a surface rupture of over 400 km was observed along the East Anatolian Fault and Sürgü-Çardak fault, described by AFAD as the biggest in Anatolia in 2000 years; the M7.8 rupture comprised ~230 km on the EAF and ~60 km on a southern branch parallel to the DSF.

Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Ground subsidence and uplift
includes.description: Shallow earthquakes can cause subsidence or uplift of the ground surface, part of the primary impacts alongside surface fault rupture and fissures. In the Türkiye earthquake, coastal inundation reported in the Iskenderun area may be related to coastal subsidence caused by the earthquake (under further investigation).

includes.label: Seismic site amplification
includes.description: Certain terrain types transmit seismic waves differently: buildings on solid bedrock are less likely to suffer damage, while those on unconsolidated rock and sediments may experience greater amplitude and duration of seismic waves, increasing damage potential. Soft clay/silt deposits (ground type S1) can produce anomalous seismic site amplification and soil-structure interaction effects requiring special study. In Myanmar, amplification effects associated with supershear rupture propagation and local geological conditions (alluvial sediments) may explain damage felt as far as Bangkok, ~1000 km from the epicentre.

includes.label: Supershear rupture propagation
includes.description: A special category of earthquake rupture where the rupture propagates along the fault plane faster than S-waves (shear waves). The M7.7 Myanmar earthquake was identified as a supershear event, with an average rupture velocity of 4.4 km/s over a rupture lasting approximately 90 seconds and extending up to 400 km, contributing to widespread seismic effects felt in Bangkok.

includes.label: Ground motion parameters (PGA, PGV, SA)
includes.description: Ground shaking intensity can be quantified through ground motion parameters such as peak ground acceleration (PGA), peak ground velocity (PGV), and elastic spectral acceleration (SA) for a given period of vibration; these are commonly measured at seismic stations and used together with the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale (I to XII, with structural damage typically beginning around VI) to describe severity of shaking effects.

includes.label: Magnitude, depth and distance effects on impact
includes.description: The impact of an earthquake depends on magnitude, depth, and distance from the epicentre. Earthquakes of M7.0 and above can cause intense shaking and serious consequences over a wide area; M6.0-6.9 may cause substantial damage in populated areas; smaller earthquakes can still damage weak structures near the epicentre. Theoretically, for two identical earthquakes differing only in depth, the deeper earthquake is expected to produce lesser surface intensity.

nodes.label: Aftershocks and foreshocks
nodes.description: Aftershocks, foreshocks and other triggered earthquakes belonging to the same seismic sequence.

includes.label: Aftershock sequence
includes.description: After a main earthquake, leftover stress along the fault line is released through a sequence of aftershocks that can occur on and off for days, weeks or even months depending on the magnitude of the mainshock. The first hours and days following an earthquake have the highest risk of new and strong earthquakes (aftershocks).

includes.label: Foreshocks
includes.description: Some earthquakes are actually foreshocks preceding a larger earthquake that might still occur; UNDAC advises awareness that an initial shock may not be the main event and a larger earthquake could follow.

includes.label: Omori's law aftershock decay
includes.description: The temporal decay of aftershock frequency can generally be characterized by Omori's law, stating that the rate of earthquakes triggered by a main shock decays with time according to an inverse power of time (1/t^p, p≈1). This explains why aftershock numbers are very high in the first days and decrease predictably afterward; magnitude-frequency relationships allow rough prediction (e.g., an M6 mainshock implies about 10 M5s, 100 M4s, etc.). This holds only for a single rupture along a single fault; a new major aftershock/rupture resets the calculations.

includes.label: Triggered earthquake via stress transfer
includes.description: A main earthquake may trigger another earthquake of considerable magnitude outside the 'predicted' aftershock area because of stress transfer along the fault system; the size, location and magnitude of such triggered events cannot be known in advance. Coulomb stress calculations after the Türkiye earthquakes showed the M7.5 second event was triggered by stress change from the M7.8 first event on the East Anatolian Fault, and stress loading was identified in sections where previous (2020 M6.7) and future earthquakes may occur.

includes.label: Predicted aftershock zone from fault geometry
includes.description: When the size and position of the fault line that generated the main earthquake is known, the area where aftershocks will occur can be roughly predicted; however triggered earthquakes due to stress transfer can occur outside this predicted zone.

includes.label: Historical case of triggered sequential earthquakes
includes.description: Less than 3 months after the M7.6 Izmit earthquake (Türkiye, 1999, >18,000 fatalities), an earthquake on the same fault system at Düzce (M7.2) caused around 1,000 fatalities; several scientific studies argued the Düzce earthquake was triggered by the stress change resulting from the Izmit earthquake, illustrating how a major earthquake can trigger another significant event on an adjacent fault segment.

includes.label: Aftershock monitoring and mapping
includes.description: Seismic networks (e.g., KOERI, USGS) continuously track and map the main shock and subsequent aftershocks, including counts by magnitude threshold (e.g., 1,054 aftershocks with 229 of M>4 as of 8 Feb 2023; 4,965 aftershocks with 368 of M>4 by 16 Feb 2023) to monitor evolving seismic hazard and inform ongoing response, including the possibility that aftershocks with M>6 cannot be excluded.

includes.label: Aftershock-induced building collapse risk
includes.description: Buildings and structures already damaged by the main shaking can become more unstable and collapse after the initial earthquake; even a small aftershock can cause collapse of an already-damaged building, posing significant risk to victims and aid workers, including damage not visible to the naked eye.

includes.label: Safety precautions during aftershocks
includes.description: UNDAC guidance recommends staying outside and at a safe distance from infrastructure throughout a mission because of ongoing aftershock risk, as aftershocks cause further damage and increase stress for victims and aid workers.

includes.label: Geoscience data collection on aftershock sequences
includes.description: Post-earthquake geoscience investigations aim to document mainshock and foreshock characteristics and aftershock sequences, alongside ground motions, to understand relationships among mainshock slip characteristics, aftershock occurrence, and site response, using tools such as lidar, InSAR, and seismic/geodetic networks.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Structural testing of mainshock-aftershock sequences
includes.description: Laboratory hybrid simulation testing of full-scale steel building frames replicates a mainshock followed by an aftershock to assess structural response; results showed that despite partial damage from the mainshock, no appreciable differences in overall seismic response were detected during the subsequent aftershock test, except one frame configuration (sprayed fire protection) which lost some dissipation capability (-12%).

nodes.label: Landslides and debris flows
nodes.description: Earthquake-induced landslides, rockfalls and debris flows affecting slopes and settlements.

includes.label: Induced landslides, rockfalls, debris flows
includes.description: A priority item for geotechnical post-earthquake data collection: induced landslides, rockfalls, and debris flows, as well as the absence of these failures in areas where they would be expected, should be documented to advance understanding of geotechnical earthquake effects.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Slope destabilization causing landslides
includes.description: Shaking from large-magnitude earthquakes can destabilize slopes, leading to landslides and debris flows, particularly in mountainous regions; this can also make access and communication difficult by damaging roads and bridges, and landslides/debris can block roads or cause surface damage.

includes.label: Landslide and slope instability hazard zoning
includes.description: In the area affected by the Molise earthquakes, the mountainous topography, geological stratification and presence of fault activity made the region prone to landslides and slope instability; a map classified the area into different levels of landslide risk (absent, low, medium, high).

includes.label: Historical settlement on landslide-prone slopes
includes.description: Historical town centres were built on elevated areas, cliffs and steep slopes for defensive reasons, limiting space for expansion without exposing new construction to landslide and slope instability dangers; human modifications such as fillings and land movements were made to allow expansion in some towns, affecting the irregular topography.

includes.label: Road sliding in cut-and-fill areas
includes.description: Following the Molise earthquakes, sliding phenomena were observed in cut and fill areas adjacent to roads with non-cohesive and compact soil that induced relative movements, causing cracks in roads such as those seen in San Giuliano di Puglia and the Vallepare area; these were caused by small land movements and localized sliding rather than superficial faults or ruptures.

includes.label: Absence of landslides on dam reservoir slopes
includes.description: Field inspections after the Molise earthquakes found that no landslides were evident on the side slopes of the Occhito dam reservoir, and no important damage was reported, illustrating a case of resilience against induced slope failures near critical infrastructure.

includes.label: Landslides as secondary earthquake hazard
includes.description: Secondary earthquake hazards, caused by primary hazards, include landslides (and debris flow), liquefaction, tsunami, seiche, flooding, fire, and ground gases, as well as technological and societal hazards; earthquakes of magnitude 7.0 and above can be expected to trigger such secondary hazards along with widespread intense ground shaking and extensive damage.

includes.label: Seismically triggered slow-moving earth slides
includes.description: Vulnerability assessment and fragility curve research address reinforced concrete buildings subjected to seismically triggered slow-moving earth slides, a specific type of landslide affecting the built environment.

includes.label: Rockfalls and landslides as environmental effects
includes.description: Earthquake-induced environmental effects include rockfalls and landslides, which were observed to cause significant soil erosion or block river streams creating quake lakes of major concern to neighbouring urban regions.

includes.label: Quake lakes from landslide river blockage
includes.description: Landslides triggered by earthquakes can block river streams, creating quake lakes that pose a major concern to neighbouring urban regions downstream.

includes.label: Landslides as cross-border cascading events
includes.description: Earthquake effects can cause cross-border impacts and cascading events, including landslides, liquefaction phenomena, tsunamis, fire, and industrial accidents, as part of the broader consequences of a single seismic event across large regions.

includes.label: Pseudo-static slope stability analysis
includes.description: Eurocode 8 requires slope stability analysis for structures located near slopes (except importance category I structures) using a pseudo-static approach where inertia forces are represented by permanent horizontal and vertical loads related to peak ground acceleration, multiplied by a topographic amplification factor; this addresses the ultimate or damage limit state related to unacceptable slope displacements.

includes.label: Topographic amplification of seismic action on slopes
includes.description: Topographic amplification factors (ST) are defined for different slope profiles (isolated cliffs/slopes, ridges) with average slope angles, ranging from 1.2 to 1.4, used to adjust peak ground acceleration for slope stability analyses near steep terrain.

nodes.label: Liquefaction
nodes.description: Soil liquefaction phenomena caused by strong shaking in saturated soils leading to ground failure.

includes.label: Soil liquefaction
includes.description: Generic term for the loss of shear strength of cohesionless (saturated) soils due to excess pore water pressure build-up caused by cyclic loading during an earthquake; the soil behaves like a liquid, causing infrastructural damage and sinking of structures. Observed in almost all significant earthquakes and extensively studied since 1964.

includes.label: Liquefaction-induced lateral spreading
includes.description: Lateral ground spreading caused by liquefaction, documented as a priority data-collection item alongside settlement and ejecta; example given of lateral spreading in the Marina district during Loma Prieta (1989) that did not damage houses directly but caused failure of gas pipelines connected to buildings.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Liquefaction settlement and ejecta
includes.description: Settlement and sand/water ejecta resulting from liquefaction are identified as key phenomena to document in post-earthquake geotechnical data collection, along with the notable absence of liquefaction in areas where it would be expected.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Liquefaction impact on buildings
includes.description: Physical impacts of liquefaction on buildings, including sinking of structures due to loss of soil bearing capacity; identified as a specific category of damage to document and illustrated by example of building damage caused by foundation soil liquefaction (Kobe 1995).

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Liquefaction damage to lifelines
includes.description: Ground failure and movements from liquefaction can damage pipelines and other lifelines; soil-foundation-structure interaction is a priority for combined geotechnical/structural/lifeline data collection; example of gas pipeline failure induced by liquefaction-related lateral spreading despite limited building damage.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Liquefaction of retaining wall backfill
includes.description: Most commonly observed failure mode of retaining structures during earthquakes is associated with liquefaction of the backfill supported by the wall; significant pore water pressure build-up must be prevented, with a minimum safety factor against liquefaction of 2.0 specified in EN 1998-5. Illustrated by example from Kobe (1995).

includes.label: Soil types susceptible to liquefaction
includes.description: Certain terrain types, especially saturated sandy sediments and cohesionless soils, can liquefy under strong shaking. Eurocode 8 defines conditions under which liquefaction assessment is not required (e.g. ground surface acceleration <0.15g combined with specific clay/silt/sand characteristics and corrected SPT blow counts), implying susceptibility otherwise.

includes.label: Liquefaction susceptibility assessment
includes.description: EN 1998-5 provides a methodology (Seed-Idriss formula for seismic demand compared with liquefaction resistance derived from SPT, CPT or shear wave velocity measurements) to reliably predict liquefaction occurrence; verification is carried out under free-field conditions reflecting conditions prevailing during the building's lifetime; recommended minimum safety factor is 1.25.

includes.label: Depth limit for liquefaction assessment
includes.description: Assessment of liquefaction is not required for soil layers located deeper than 15 m below the foundation elevation in EN 1998-5, though susceptibility to liquefaction decreases but does not disappear with depth; this condition should be complemented by consideration of relative foundation dimensions, which the code does not fully address.

includes.label: Ground type classification for liquefaction risk
includes.description: EN 1998-1 ground type classification (soil profiles S1 and S2) requires special studies when ground conditions indicate possible liquefaction or soil failure under seismic action; liquefaction normally leads to catastrophic failures of structures as the soil loses bearing capacity, causing collapse of foundations previously relying on it.

includes.label: Ground investigation to identify liquefaction risk
includes.description: EN 1998-1/EN 1998-5 require in-situ or laboratory investigations to identify ground conditions and detect possible occurrence of soil behaviour detrimental to structures, including permanent settlements caused by liquefaction or densification; if risks are identified, mitigation measures must be taken or the construction site reconsidered.

includes.label: Partial loss of soil strength (non-liquefied state)
includes.description: Excess pore water pressure build-up can cause a significant loss of soil strength during seismic loading even without reaching full liquefaction state, affecting slope stability calculations; sensitive clays may also show sudden strength drops beyond a strain threshold.

includes.label: Liquefaction as secondary earthquake hazard
includes.description: Liquefaction is classified as a secondary earthquake hazard (caused by primary hazards such as ground shaking), alongside landslides/debris flow, tsunami, seiche, flooding, fire and ground gases, as well as technological and societal hazards.

includes.label: Post-earthquake liquefaction reconnaissance
includes.description: Priority geotechnical data-collection item after earthquakes is documenting liquefaction and its effects (lateral spreading, settlement, ejecta), including instances where liquefaction was absent in areas where it would be expected, to advance empirical methodologies for engineering codes and guidelines; this is coordinated by bodies such as GEER in collaboration with EERI, NIST and USGS.

nodes.label: Tsunami and seiche
nodes.description: Tsunami waves and seiche effects generated by submarine or coastal earthquakes.

includes.label: Tsunami generation by earthquakes
includes.description: A tsunami is a series of ocean waves caused by earthquakes (accounting for 80% of occurrences) or other phenomena such as volcanic eruptions, underwater landslides, coastal rock falls and meteorite impacts, leading to significant water displacement in the ocean. It is a complex event that can last many hours; a tsunami consists of multiple waves in succession and the first wave is not always the largest. Earthquakes occurring near coasts or oceans can cause tsunamis, which can be extremely destructive and increase overall disaster impact.

includes.label: Subduction-zone megathrust tsunamis
includes.description: When earthquakes occur in regions where tectonic plates converge and one plate subducts beneath another, the resulting tsunamis can be exceptionally catastrophic in size and impact; tsunami waves can grow to enormous dimensions and travel across entire ocean basins with very little energy loss, much faster than wind-generated waves.

includes.label: Exposure of low-elevation coastal areas
includes.description: Locations situated at sea level are particularly vulnerable to tsunami events; critical infrastructure such as ports and airports may become unusable due to the severity of the earthquake and/or tsunami.

includes.label: Seiche waves on inland water bodies
includes.description: Tsunami-like seiche waves can impact areas close to large bodies of water, generated by earthquake shaking; earthquakes can also change the course of rivers and result in flash floods.

includes.label: Tsunami early warning systems
includes.description: Earthquake parameters (location, depth, magnitude) detected through seismic networks assist Tsunami Early Warning Centres to determine the tsunamigenic potential of an earthquake; warnings are pushed to threatened coastal areas, sometimes providing hours of lead time to evacuate. For earthquakes close to coastal areas such advance warning may not be possible, and the occurrence of a strong or long earthquake should itself be interpreted as a natural sign for self-evacuation. NOAA's U.S. Tsunami Warning System website shows alert levels (e.g. WARNING level).

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Probabilistic tsunami hazard assessment
includes.description: Scientific methods and models (e.g. global and regional probabilistic tsunami hazard assessments, inundation maps, event-tree models) are used to quantify tsunami hazard from earthquake sources, including source uncertainty quantification and accuracy/feasibility studies of inundation maps for coastal regions such as the Mediterranean.

includes.label: Tsunami structural fragility assessment
includes.description: Tsunami vulnerability of critical infrastructure (e.g. RC buildings, steel structures such as warehouses and cranes) is assessed via nonlinear static time-history analyses accounting for inundation depth, deriving fragility curves describing the probability of exceeding predefined damage states as a function of tsunami intensity; results show seismic and tsunami capacity curves predict similar damage state limits.

includes.label: Tsunami warnings and bulletins after major earthquake
includes.description: After the M7.8 Türkiye earthquake, tsunami warnings were issued followed by bulletins related to tsunami observations in Türkiye and Cyprus, with wave heights of less than 20cm observed; no significant tsunami inundation or impact occurred.

includes.label: Tsunami-caused damage in earthquake alert classification
includes.description: International earthquake impact categorization systems (e.g. NEHRP significant domestic earthquake levels) explicitly consider damage caused by tsunami when assigning impact levels: Level 1 is used for an international earthquake causing significant damage in the US including damage from a tsunami (designated WARNING alert on NOAA Tsunami Warning System), and Level 2 for moderate tsunami-related damage.

includes.label: Tsunami as secondary earthquake hazard
includes.description: Tsunami and seiche are classified among secondary earthquake hazards caused by primary hazards (alongside landslides, liquefaction, flooding, fire and ground gases), as well as technological and societal hazards.

nodes.label: Dam failure and flooding
nodes.description: Dam breach, dam failure and resulting downstream flooding triggered by earthquake damage.

includes.label: Dam/embankment failure mechanisms
includes.description: Dams, embankments, and levees may fail during an earthquake due to cracks and instability, causing downstream flooding. Failure can result from overtopping, internal erosion, or accumulated damage to dam and foundation not always linked to overtopping; earthquakes are cited as one cause of such failures alongside internal erosion.

includes.label: Dam-break wave downstream flooding
includes.description: Following a dam failure, an uncontrolled release of the reservoir sends a large amount of water downstream in the form of a dam-break wave, travelling extremely fast with enormous eroding and transport capacity. Impact depends on failure mechanism, reservoir volume, dam height/type, downstream land occupation, and population exposure. Historical large dam failures have caused death tolls ranging from hundreds to tens of thousands of people.

includes.label: Dam structural cracking from shaking
includes.description: Severe earthquake shaking can cause longitudinal and other structural cracks in dam bodies, as observed at an earth-fill dam where cracks appeared along the structure and reservoir level had to be managed through controlled discharge; similar cracking was reported at another dam in northwest Syria, prompting evacuation concerns.

includes.label: Dam breach inundation modelling
includes.description: Rapid hydrodynamic modelling (e.g. using the NAMIDANCE shallow water/tsunami code adapted for dam breach simulation) is used to estimate flood wave arrival times, inundation extent, flow depths and exposed population downstream of at-risk dams after an earthquake. Simulations use topography (SRTM30/SRTM-GL1/GL3), reservoir bathymetry datasets (GLOBathy, Global Dam Watch, ICOLD) and assume complete or partial dam collapse scenarios; results are described as order-of-magnitude estimates rather than precise indications.

includes.label: Controlled reservoir drawdown/discharge
includes.description: When dam integrity is compromised, controlled discharge or drawdown orders may be issued to reduce reservoir levels and prevent further damage or failure; drawdown orders are typically triggered if the dam is severely/critically damaged or the spillway is severely damaged. In one case, a damaged earth-fill dam's reservoir level was reduced via controlled discharge and the dam was being evacuated.

includes.label: Downstream population exposure to dam breach
includes.description: Rapid scenario analyses estimate large numbers of people potentially exposed to flooding in case of dam breach, including figures for people reached within specific timeframes (e.g. first hour, few hours) and at different flood depths. One scenario estimated around 103,000 people exposed, with 15,000 within one hour and additional 17,000 within two hours, and about 24,000-28,000 exposed to flood depths greater than 4m/1m respectively; total flooded area and built-up area are also quantified.

includes.label: Dam vulnerability to seismic shaking
includes.description: Vulnerability functions for dam-reservoir system elements (dam body, spillway, bottom outlet, hydropower system) to earthquake shaking are defined via damage states based on structural integrity loss; embankment dams are considered particularly resilient, with full reservoir release only expected for very rare return period events (e.g. assumed to fail at ~1,000,000 year return period in one study), while spillways may be damaged at much more frequent return periods (e.g. 475 years).

includes.label: Satellite-based dam breach scenario mapping
includes.description: Copernicus Emergency Management Service (CEMS) Risk and Recovery Mapping activations are used after an earthquake to perform detailed dam break and discharge scenario modelling, including reference datasets of flood-prone areas, IDP camp identification, flood inundation mapping, and exposure assessment of citizens and infrastructure under worst-case (complete dam wall collapse) and medium-risk (partial break) scenarios.

includes.label: Flooding from controlled dam discharge vs dam collapse
includes.description: Downstream flooding after an earthquake may result either from an actual dam collapse or from the controlled opening of a dam for water discharge combined with damage to water infrastructures along the river caused by shaking and aftershocks; distinguishing the actual cause of flooding requires field validation as satellite-detected flooding alone cannot confirm dam collapse.

includes.label: Prioritisation of critical dams for assessment
includes.description: Dams are prioritised for rapid post-earthquake assessment based on factors such as proximity to the epicentre, level of shaking intensity experienced (e.g. Modified Mercalli Intensity VII), large reservoir capacity, presence of multiple downstream populated areas, and field reports of structural cracks from humanitarian teams.

includes.label: Compounding factors complicating dam breach response
includes.description: Response to a potential dam breach can be complicated by additional factors such as the presence of landmines near the dam area, ongoing armed conflict in the region, and lack of real-time data on current reservoir water levels, all of which hinder accurate impact assessment and response planning.

nodes.label: Fire following earthquake
nodes.description: Fires ignited as a consequence of earthquake damage to structures, gas or electrical systems.

includes.label: Gas and electrical system ignition
includes.description: Damage to infrastructure following an earthquake can result in the release of flammable liquids or gases; ruptured power cables and natural gas lines can ignite fires when in contact with ignition sources. Heating and cooking appliances may also be overturned, triggering destructive fires during and after the earthquake.

includes.label: Impaired firefighting due to water outage
includes.description: Fire damages may be compounded if water lines are also broken during the earthquake, as there will not be enough water to extinguish fires once they have started.

includes.label: Industrial/port facility fire
includes.description: A major port was partially damaged by the earthquake, toppling dozens of containers; a major fire erupted, possibly originating from flammable industrial oil or chemicals in a container, halting all port operations. The fire was extinguished using combined land, sea and air efforts, but damage and structural issues delayed resumption of operations; toppled containers also hampered emergency services access.

includes.label: Fire following earthquake (FFE) phenomenon
includes.description: Fires following earthquake (FFE) have historically produced large post-earthquake damage and losses in terms of lives, buildings and economic costs, as seen in the San Francisco (1906), Kobe (1995), Turkey (1999), Tohoku (2011) and Christchurch (2011) earthquakes. FFE pose a considerable threat as they can be widespread at building and regional level owing to rupture of gas lines, failure of electrical systems, and failure of fire compartmentation measures.

includes.label: Disrupted firefighting response capacity
includes.description: Post-earthquake fires are more difficult for fire brigades to tackle because of their possible large number and extent, disruptions within the infrastructural network and the water supply system that hinder timely intervention, and because fire brigades must also be engaged in rescue operations after the earthquake.

includes.label: Fire acting on seismically damaged structure
includes.description: The structural fire performance can worsen significantly because fire acts on an already damaged structure; passive and active fire protections may themselves have been damaged by seismic action, and fire can spread quickly if compartmentation measures have failed. The loss of fire protection is particularly dangerous for steel structures due to high thermal conductivity and small profile thicknesses, leading to quick temperature rise.

includes.label: Seismic performance of passive fire protection systems
includes.description: Experimental tests on calcium silicate boards (standard and seismic-designed), spray-based fire protection and firewalls (with and without seismic detailing) showed that fire protections and firewalls did not suffer major damage owing to cyclic/seismic loading, and damage was not likely to significantly affect fire performance; minimizing non-structural damage is key to preserving structural fire performance after an earthquake.

includes.label: Prior research on FFE structural fragility
includes.description: Cited prior research documents reduced fire resistance after seismic damage: e.g. fire door sets showed up to 70% decrease in fire resistance after cyclic (earthquake-simulated) loading; full-scale RC frames tested for fire after seismic damage showed seismic damage affected the rise in temperatures in structural elements; various studies examined post-earthquake fire performance of steel, composite and concrete-filled tube columns, connections, and sprinkler piping systems.

nodes.label: Technological and Natech accidents
nodes.description: Technological accidents and Natech events such as hazardous material releases or industrial accidents triggered by earthquakes.

includes.label: Hazardous material release from damaged installations
includes.description: Technological accidents can be triggered by earthquakes, which can damage hazardous installations and release hazardous substances, leading to fires or explosions, gas leaks, damaged facilities, chemical spills, etc.

includes.label: Industrial accident triggered by earthquake
includes.description: Natech event defined as an industrial accident triggered by the damage induced by a natural event; STREST addresses seismic performance/loss assessment of site-specific high consequence facilities such as oil refineries and petrochemical plants where natural-event triggered ruptures of equipment (atmospheric tanks, pressurised equipment, pipelines) may result in severe accidental scenarios (fires, explosions, toxic releases).

includes.label: Rupture of hazardous process equipment
includes.description: Equipment processing or storing flammable/toxic/highly flammable or extremely flammable/toxic substances (atmospheric tanks, pressurised vessels, spheres, pipelines) can rupture under seismic shaking, releasing hazardous substances; earthquake-triggered structural damage to water tanks is similar to that of tanks containing hazardous materials.

includes.label: Natech risk assessment methodology
includes.description: References note the extension of quantitative industrial risk assessment to earthquake effects and a hazard matrix developed for risk assessment of chemical process equipment under seismic loading, as well as reviews of risk analysis methods for Natech events.

includes.label: Port container fire after earthquake
includes.description: A major port in Iskenderun was partially damaged by the earthquake, toppling dozens of containers; a major fire erupted among hundreds of shipping containers, halting all port operations for days. The cause was unclear, with speculation over flammable industrial oil or chemicals; the fire was eventually extinguished using combined land, sea and air efforts, but reignited and required days of cooling and rehabilitation before operations resumed.

includes.label: Aftershock-triggered industrial release risk
includes.description: Ongoing shallow aftershocks with high magnitude may cause further damage to industrial structures and equipment that were damaged but had not yet released hazardous substances, potentially triggering delayed releases.

includes.label: Asbestos release from earthquake-damaged buildings
includes.description: Obsolete buildings containing asbestos-containing materials (ACM) may be damaged by earthquakes, releasing asbestos fibres into the atmosphere as a long-term health hazard; this is defined as a natural-technologic (na-tech) event. Measurements after the Great Hanshin earthquake showed fibre concentrations above acceptable limits even 36 hours after simulated damage, and the pre-event stock of sprayed-on asbestos (3740 tonnes) resulted in about 26.4 kg released into the environment, contributing to increased pneumonia cases.

includes.label: Asbestos contamination during demolition and clean-up
includes.description: Post-earthquake building waste containing asbestos must be separated from demolition waste for disposal, reuse or recycling; asbestos waste is easily mixed with other debris and often not visible, so improper demolition or clean-up (or burnt asbestos material) can increase local asbestos exposure, threatening the health of workers and occupants during repair of damaged buildings.

includes.label: Combined seismic-asbestos exposure risk mapping
includes.description: Seismic risk combined with asbestos presence in residential buildings is used to identify EU regions where seismic activity may trigger increased asbestos exposure due to damage of the built environment; high seismic risk and high asbestos use overlap notably in Italy and Cyprus, with secondary hotspots in Austria, Bulgaria, France, Germany, Slovenia and Hungary, guiding prioritisation for asbestos screening, registration and remediation.

includes.label: Cascading industrial accidents and business interruption
includes.description: Earthquakes can cause cross-border impacts and cascading events including industrial accidents and business interruption, alongside tsunamis, landslides, liquefaction and fire; secondary damage from earthquakes can result in Natech events such as release of hazardous materials and destruction of vital transport and technical infrastructure, industrial buildings and facilities, with earthquakes among the most common hazards addressed in Natech risk assessment.

includes.label: Air pollution from burning chemicals
includes.description: Earthquake secondary effects include air pollution due to the burning of chemicals, following damage to industrial or chemical storage facilities.

nodes.label: Damage to buildings
nodes.description: Structural and non-structural damage or collapse of residential, commercial and public buildings.

includes.label: Soft storey collapse
includes.description: Partial or total collapse of soft storeys was a common damage mechanism observed in old reinforced concrete buildings, together with shear damage of short columns and damage of beam-column joints.

includes.label: Masonry infill damage
includes.description: Diagonal cracking, separation from beams and columns, and partial or out-of-plane collapse of masonry infills was observed extensively in both old and new reinforced concrete buildings; this damage required costly repair and in some cases blocked emergency exits in public buildings, rendering them unusable even without other structural damage.

includes.label: Out-of-plane façade collapse
includes.description: Continuous two-leaf masonry façades lacking connection between leaves collapsed out-of-plane in both old and new reinforced concrete buildings; this is a potential cause of injury and asset damage, and can block emergency exits.

includes.label: Pounding damage between adjacent buildings
includes.description: Adjacent buildings with floors not coinciding in elevation suffered severe pounding damage at the storey corresponding to the roof of the stiffer neighbouring building, illustrating insufficient conceptual design.

includes.label: Structural irregularity-induced damage
includes.description: Horizontal and vertical irregularities (frames arranged in only one direction, slabs built at different heights following slope, elimination of structural elements during reconstruction, uneven distribution of mass/stiffness/strength) contributed to collapse or severe damage in both old and new buildings.

includes.label: Non-structural component damage
includes.description: Non-structural elements (partitions, ceilings, balconies, roof tiles, mechanical/electrical/plumbing components, furniture and contents) are frequently damaged or collapse, posing safety risks to pedestrians, causing high repair costs and long restoration times, and in some damage states (Near Collapse) most non-structural components have collapsed.

includes.label: Damage to churches and heritage buildings
includes.description: Churches and monuments proved very vulnerable to seismic loads, experiencing collapse of bell towers, drums, façades, roofs and naves; heritage sites in old city centres (e.g. 83% of religious sites in a case study area) were damaged to varying extents.

includes.label: Masonry building collapse
includes.description: Old masonry buildings, especially those with poor quality materials or previous incorrect restoration/retrofitting, suffered extensive damage or complete collapse; heavy replacement roofs increasing mass, unconnected corners, and unanchored arches were recurrent causes of collapse.

includes.label: Higher vulnerability of old buildings
includes.description: Old reinforced concrete and masonry buildings (constituting over 80% of examined stock in one case) performed far worse than new buildings, which suffered mainly non-structural damage but no collapses, demonstrating a clear age-related vulnerability gradient.

includes.label: Graded structural damage states
includes.description: Buildings experience defined limit states of damage from Damage Limitation (light, economically repairable) to Significant Damage (moderate drifts, likely uneconomic to repair) to Near Collapse (heavily damaged, low residual strength, large permanent drifts, unlikely to survive another earthquake), used to classify post-earthquake building condition.

includes.label: Fragility-based damage classification
includes.description: Building damage is classified using fragility/vulnerability functions into categories such as minor, moderate, major, complete damage, collapsed and washed away, with building height and material type affecting the degree of damage; damage factors represent the share of reconstruction cost needed to repair each damage state.

includes.label: Widespread damage threshold (MMI VIII+)
includes.description: Areas experiencing Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) values equal to or greater than VIII are associated with widespread building damage, a threshold used for post-earthquake building data collection and loss estimation.

includes.label: Mass building collapse with high death/damage toll
includes.description: In the Türkiye and Syria earthquakes, more than 300 buildings collapsed in government-controlled Syria, with 169 classified high risk and 644 medium risk of collapse in Aleppo; in north-west Syria over 8,900 buildings were completely or partially destroyed; in Türkiye damage was estimated at USD 84.1 billion with around 230 million tons of debris generated.

includes.label: Damage concentrated in informal settlements
includes.description: Most small settlements in the affected Syrian area fell into the 'informal settlement' typology, presenting structural vulnerability factors that exacerbated earthquake damage, compounded in some areas by pre-existing conflict damage reducing buildings' ability to withstand shaking.

includes.label: Repair cost and economic loss from damage
includes.description: Damage-loss models define damage factors as the share of construction/replacement cost required to repair each damage state for structural and non-structural components and contents; the European Seismic Risk Model applies this across four damage states (slight, moderate, extensive, complete), with an EU case study estimating 3.1 billion euro/year repair cost in residential buildings across 100 prioritised regions.

includes.label: Building collapse as primary casualty cause
includes.description: More than 75% of deaths in past earthquakes were due to building collapse, with lethality depending on ground motion characteristics, building type, collapse mechanism, occupancy and search-and-rescue effectiveness.

includes.label: Post-earthquake instability and collapse risk from aftershocks
includes.description: Buildings damaged by shaking can become more unstable and collapse after the initial earthquake, even from small aftershocks; damage may not always be visible to the naked eye, posing ongoing safety risks for occupants and responders.

includes.label: Terrain-amplified building damage
includes.description: Buildings on unconsolidated rock and sediments may experience greater amplitude and duration of seismic waves than those on solid bedrock, increasing damage potential; degree of damage also depends on soil conditions and building irregularities.

includes.label: Business interruption from building damage
includes.description: Financial loss arises from building downtime, comprising mobilisation time (damage assessment, contractor bidding, debris clean-up, financing) and repair time, leading to loss of rental income, business revenue or relocation costs.

nodes.label: Damage to bridges and viaducts
nodes.description: Damage to bridges, viaducts and other transport structures from seismic shaking.

includes.label: Shear cracking in pier transverse beams
includes.description: PsD testing of an old RC viaduct (Rio Torto) with portal frame piers showed significant shear crack patterns developing in the transverse beams of piers under ULS and beyond-design (200% ULS) seismic loading, with pinching behaviour and progressive degradation of the hysteretic response.

includes.description: Testing revealed significant crack opening at the base section of viaduct pier columns (base-column opening) during seismic cycles, associated with bond slip of plain steel reinforcement bars and a fix-end rotation effect causing alternating opening/closing of cracks and stiffness variation.

includes.description: The predominant mode of failure identified for older RC viaduct piers (designed chiefly for gravity loads, with plain steel bars and inadequate seismic detailing) is shear failure of the transverse beams, confirmed by both full-scale and 1:4 scale pier testing.

includes.label: Non-uniform damage distribution in old bridges
includes.description: Tests on an older highway bridge pier (poorly detailed, designed without seismic provisions) revealed poor seismic behaviour, with non-uniform distribution of damage and sudden changes in damage patterns for increasing amplitudes of ground motion; undesirable failure locations occurred above curtailed vertical reinforcement due to tension shift combined with shear cracking.

includes.label: Highway viaduct undamaged by shaking
includes.description: Small-to-medium RC viaducts on the main motorway linking the Molise earthquake-affected area did not suffer any significant damage from the 2002 seismic sequence.

includes.label: Localized road cracking from ground movement
includes.description: Cracks observed in local roads after the earthquake were caused not by surface faulting or rupture but by small land movements and localized sliding, especially in cut-and-fill areas with non-cohesive, compact soils adjacent to roads.

includes.label: Destruction of roads and bridges hampering access
includes.description: Destruction of roads, bridges and other infrastructure caused by earthquake shaking can make access and communication difficult for response operations, compounding the effects of landslides and debris blocking roads.

nodes.label: Damage to lifelines
nodes.description: Damage to power, water, gas, telecommunications and other lifeline infrastructure networks.

includes.label: Power infrastructure damage
includes.description: Earthquakes damage electrical infrastructure including power lines and substations, causing blackouts; in Türkiye, approximately 30 TEIAŞ substations suffered varying degrees of damage, and multiple districts (Osmaniye Bahçe-Düziçi, Kahramanmaraş city centre, Malatya, Akçadağ, Doğanşehir, Doğanyol) were reported out of electricity. Power cables can be ruptured, severed or extensively damaged by shaking.

includes.label: Gas pipeline rupture
includes.description: Natural gas transmission and distribution lines can be ruptured by earthquake shaking. In the Türkiye earthquake, the state-owned BOTAS natural gas transmission pipeline in Hatay Province ruptured in two sections roughly 3 km apart, with the worst damage in Turkoglu district near the epicentre, affecting the main line supplying Marash, Gaziantep, Hatay and Kilis. Gas lines can be ruptured, severed or extensively damaged, hampering relief efforts and daily living.

includes.label: Gas explosion and fire from pipeline rupture
includes.description: Rupture of gas transmission pipelines caused explosions and fires at the two rupture points in Hatay Province, Türkiye, with flame heights estimated around 30 meters (100 ft); fires from the ruptures were later extinguished.

includes.label: Precautionary gas supply shutdown
includes.description: As a precaution following pipeline rupture, natural gas flows on the Kahramanmaras-Gaziantep transmission line were halted to Gaziantep, Hatay and Kahramanmaras provinces and nearby districts (Pazarcık, Narlı, Besni, Gölbaşı, Nurdağı, Islahiye, Reyhanlı, Kırıkhan, Hassa) near the epicentre as a result of the pipeline damage, while BOTAŞ technical teams carried out field controls and interventions.

includes.label: Telecommunications network damage
includes.description: Earthquakes can rupture or extensively damage telecommunications systems, isolating people and preventing coordination; damaged communications systems hamper relief efforts and day-to-day living.

includes.label: Water and sanitation infrastructure damage
includes.description: Water and sanitation pipes can be ruptured, severed or extensively damaged by earthquakes. In Syria, water disruptions due to contamination affected rural areas of Aleppo, and water stations, reservoirs and tanks were damaged in many areas, worsening the health situation amid an ongoing cholera outbreak.

includes.label: Lifeline interdependency and cascading effects
includes.description: Damage to one lifeline system can have multitude of cascading effects on the flow of resources within communities, leading to significant social and economic impacts at regional, national and global scale. Post-earthquake investigations should identify inter-system dependencies among different lifeline systems and recognize indirect and cascading impacts (positive or negative) of lifelines damage and disruption.

includes.label: Lifeline systems classification
includes.description: Principal infrastructure lifeline systems identified by ASCE Infrastructure Resilience Division include communications, electric power, natural gas and liquid fuels, potable water, solid waste management, storm water drainage, transportation, and wastewater. FEMA's broader community lifelines categories include safety and security; food, water, and shelter; health and medical; energy; communications; transportation; and hazardous materials.

includes.label: Direct physical and operational damage to lifelines
includes.description: Post-earthquake investigations document details of direct physical and operational damage to lifeline systems, including disruption and resilience of the network of assets, services and capabilities, resulting from fault rupture, ground shaking, landslides, liquefaction, fire-following earthquakes, and tsunamis.

includes.label: Identification of critical lifeline components
includes.description: Post-earthquake investigations identify system elements or components that proved to be critical to the post-earthquake functioning of lifeline systems, informing future resilience improvements.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Seismic fragility of distribution networks
includes.description: Distributed critical infrastructures such as gas distribution networks are modelled as graphs of nodes (stations, regulator groups, joints) and links (pipes), with fragility curves for pipelines and stations used to calculate performance indicators such as Serviceability loss and Connectivity loss under seismic hazard (ground shaking and liquefaction), as applied in the SYNER-G methodology for gas networks.

includes.label: Documentation of lifeline restoration time
includes.description: Post-earthquake investigations detail post-earthquake restoration and repair activities for lifeline systems, including time to restore basic intended functions and service capabilities.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Port infrastructure damage
includes.description: A major port in the Mediterranean coastal city of Iskenderun, Türkiye, was partially damaged by the earthquake, with dozens of containers toppled, affecting port operations as a lifeline/critical infrastructure.

includes.label: Fire damage compounded by water line disruption
includes.description: Fire damages from earthquake-triggered ignitions may be compounded when water lines are also broken during the earthquake, as there will not be enough water to extinguish the fires once they have started.

includes.label: Hospital power outages
includes.description: Hospitals could face power outages that could lead to the death of patients in intensive care units as a consequence of damaged electrical lifeline infrastructure.

includes.label: Surface faulting disruption of lifelines
includes.description: Surface faulting and ground failure can cause the disruption of tunnels, railroads, power lines, water supply networks and other lifelines.

nodes.label: Damage to critical facilities
nodes.description: Damage to critical and industrial facilities including hospitals, schools, ports, airports and dams.

includes.label: Collapse of school buildings
includes.description: Collapse of a school building (Scuola Francesco Jovine, San Giuliano di Puglia) caused the death of 26 children out of 29 total casualties; the building was a mixed RC-masonry structure, originally designed in the 1950s with an upper storey added later without seismic analysis required by law.

includes.label: Hospital collapse or damage
includes.description: Severe damage to critical infrastructure recorded, in particular two hospitals collapsed; hospitals could also face power outages leading to death of ICU patients, and hospital personnel may abandon duty posts.

includes.label: Airport damage/closure
includes.description: Critical infrastructure such as airports may become unusable due to the severity of an earthquake; Hatay airport was reported out of service after the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes.

includes.label: Port damage and fire
includes.description: A major port in the Mediterranean coastal city of Iskenderun was partially damaged by the earthquake, with dozens of containers toppled. A major fire erupted at the port, bringing operations to a halt; the fire engulfed hundreds of shipping containers, forcing diversion of freight liners and halting all terminal operations until damage assessment was completed.

includes.label: Dam damage and breach risk
includes.description: Dams may fail during an earthquake, causing downstream flooding due to cracks and instability; large dams exposed to strong shaking were identified and modelled for breach scenarios (e.g. Sultansuyu, Maydanki/Afrin, Yarseli Baraji dams in Türkiye/Syria; Sedawgyi Dam in Myanmar), with a total dam breach potentially affecting 100,000 people in one case.

includes.label: Damage to electrical substations
includes.description: Approximately 30 substations belonging to Türkiye's Electricity Transmission Corporation (TEIAŞ) suffered varying degrees of damage, causing blackouts in multiple cities and districts (Osmaniye Bahçe-Düziçi, Kahramanmaraş city centre, Malatya, Akçadağ, Doğanşehir, Doğanyol).

includes.label: Natural gas transmission pipeline rupture
includes.description: The state-owned natural gas transmission pipeline (operated by BOTAŞ) in Hatay Province was ruptured in two sections roughly 3 km apart due to earthquake shaking, with the biggest damage near Turkoglu district close to the epicentre; this line fed Marash, Gaziantep, Hatay and Kilis, causing explosions and fires with flame heights around 30 metres, and necessitating halted gas flows and precautionary measures.

includes.label: Oil terminal and pipeline damage
includes.description: Operations were suspended at the Ceyhan oil terminal (150 km from epicentre) due to reported damage and spills from storage tanks; a small leak was stopped. The Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) crude oil pipeline was damaged at connection points of two berths, with oil flow halted under force majeure and the terminal control room damaged, delaying reopening.

includes.label: Damage to industrial facilities
includes.description: Critical infrastructure assessment frameworks address site-specific high-consequence industrial facilities (e.g. oil refineries and petrochemical plants) where seismic damage and triggered effects (e.g. industrial accidents) generate the main loss, as direct damage is typically a negligible fraction compared to cascading consequences.

includes.label: Port infrastructure damage (general)
includes.description: Port infrastructures are classified as critical facilities for which vulnerability assessment and fragility curves have been developed, covering components such as port buildings and cranes exposed to seismic hazard.

includes.label: Lifeline network vulnerability (pipelines)
includes.description: Distributed critical infrastructures such as major hydrocarbon pipelines are vulnerable to seismic shaking, where local failure can imply lifeline interruption over large areas, with downtime as the main cause of loss and potential for triggered hazardous material release accidents.

includes.label: Mass-scale building collapse
includes.description: At a national scale, a major earthquake sequence severely damaged or collapsed approximately 233,000 buildings, illustrating the extent of critical and residential facility damage possible from a single seismic event.

nodes.label: Deaths and injuries
nodes.description: Fatalities, injuries and people trapped under rubble resulting directly from the earthquake.

includes.label: Trauma deaths from building collapse
includes.description: UNDAC notes that trauma resulting from building collapse or other seismic activity is the leading cause of death after an earthquake, accounting for up to 75-80% of fatalities. The national seismic risk guide similarly reports that more than 75% of deaths in past events were due to building collapse, using a 'lethality ratio' (people killed to people present) to estimate casualties per building class.

includes.label: Low mortality outdoors
includes.description: UNDAC notes that death is rare for people who are outside a building at the time of the earthquake.

includes.label: People trapped under rubble
includes.description: Structural collapses generate trapped victims who may survive for several days; under special ideal conditions (food, water, temperate climate) survival may extend considerably, but 85-95% of persons rescued alive from collapsed buildings are rescued in the first 24-48 hours after an earthquake.

includes.label: Spectrum of injuries including crush syndrome
includes.description: Most post-earthquake injuries are minor cuts and bruises, followed by simple bone fractures, and a minority with multiple severe fractures and internal injuries requiring surgery and intensive treatment for crush syndrome. Within 3-5 days most injured arrive at medical facilities, often in two waves (local casualties first, then referred cases from farther areas); victims of secondary hazards such as aftershocks and fires may arrive later.

includes.label: Missing persons
includes.description: Reports of people still missing following an earthquake, e.g. over 300 missing persons across Myanmar (UN OCHA/MSF) and 78 missing people in Thailand after the Myanmar earthquake.

includes.label: Reported earthquake fatalities
includes.description: Official and NGO death tolls reported and updated over time for the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes: 1,498 fatalities in Türkiye and 685 in government-controlled Syria (plus 380 in rebel-held NW Syria) on 6 Feb; rising to 18,991 fatalities in Türkiye and 1,347 (government areas)/2,030 (rebel-controlled areas) in Syria by 10 Feb; and reaching an estimated 72,663 fatalities in Türkiye (TURKONFED estimate) and more than 5,800 deaths in Syria by 17 Feb.

includes.label: Reported earthquake injuries
includes.description: Numbers of injured people reported and updated for the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes: 8,533 injured in Türkiye and 2,126 (plus ~1,000 in rebel-held areas) in Syria on 6 Feb; rising to 75,523 injured in Türkiye and 2,295 (government)/2,950 (rebel-controlled) in Syria by 10 Feb; reaching 14,500 injured in Syria by 17 Feb.

includes.label: Reported Myanmar earthquake fatalities
includes.description: More than 3,000 fatalities reported in Myanmar as of 1 April (worst-hit Mandalay city area with nearly 1,800 deaths); earlier WHO figures (30 March) cited 402 deaths in Naypyidaw, 314 in Sagaing, 79 in Southern Shan state and 35 in Bago. Neighbouring countries also reported fatalities: 19 in Thailand and 2 injured, none reported dead, in China's Yunnan province by 1-2 April.

includes.label: Reported Myanmar earthquake injuries
includes.description: Around 3,900 injured people reported across Myanmar as of 1-2 April; 34 injured in Thailand and 2 injured in China's Yunnan province.

includes.label: Child fatalities from school collapse
includes.description: The Molise field mission reported that the collapse of the 'Scuola Francesco Jovine' school in San Giuliano di Puglia during the 2002 earthquake wiped out the lives of most of the town's six and seven-year-old children, with Italian prosecutors investigating why the school collapsed.

includes.label: Rapid fatality estimation (PAGER)
includes.description: The USGS PAGER system produces rapid post-earthquake alerts estimating population exposed to shaking and likely fatalities/economic losses (illustrated for the 2018 Anchorage M7.1 earthquake), used to categorize event significance and guide response decisions.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Cumulative global earthquake death toll
includes.description: Nearly 830,000 people were killed during earthquakes and associated secondary hazardous events between 1994 and 2024, mainly due to physical (fragile building construction) and/or social (age, health conditions) vulnerability (CRED, 2024).

includes.label: Casualty estimation models
includes.description: Injuries and casualties during earthquakes are caused by structural and non-structural damage, accidents, heart attacks, etc. Numerous casualty models of varying sophistication have been developed based on past-event observations and expert input, providing estimates of the percentage of people lightly, moderately, seriously injured or killed following an earthquake.

nodes.label: Disease and mental health effects
nodes.description: Disease outbreaks and psychological or mental health consequences among affected populations.

includes.label: Disease outbreaks after earthquakes
includes.description: Diseases and mortality rates in the weeks following an earthquake depend largely on the occurrence of epidemics; outbreaks are unlikely and usually of very modest proportions, though in Türkiye/Syria a pre-existing cholera outbreak worsened (19 438 cases in Aleppo, 16 366 in Ar-Raqqa as of 31 January 2023) and there was concern for new/worsened outbreaks of waterborne and communicable diseases due to water shortages and poor sanitation/hygiene conditions.

includes.label: Cholera outbreak
includes.description: Syria was facing a pre-existing cholera outbreak (19 438 cases registered in Aleppo, 23% of total, and 16 366 in Ar-Raqqa, 19% of total, as of 31 January 2023) which, combined with many bodies still trapped under buildings, was expected to cause a serious worsening of the already poor health situation. Shortage of cholera vaccines worldwide was reported as a possible negative factor for the crisis.

includes.label: Waterborne and communicable disease risk
includes.description: Public health experts and NGOs warned of high risk of new or exacerbated outbreaks of waterborne and other communicable diseases due to water shortages and poor sanitation/hygiene conditions in both Türkiye and Syria; rural areas of Aleppo faced water disruptions due to contamination of damaged water stations, reservoirs and tanks.

includes.label: Scabies outbreak
includes.description: Local media reported a scabies outbreak among adults in Adiyaman, Türkiye, in the weeks following the earthquake.

includes.label: Gastrointestinal symptoms in children
includes.description: NGOs reported children in Antakya, Türkiye, experiencing symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea, possibly associated with the spread of a communicable disease.

includes.label: Asbestos-related disease risk
includes.description: Collapse or damage of buildings containing asbestos-containing materials can release asbestos fibres into the air at concentrations above acceptable limits (even 36 hours after collapse), posing a health hazard for workers and residents; historical cases show considerable risk of asbestos-related disease such as mesothelioma among first responders and exposed populations, and increased pneumonia cases linked to airborne asbestos after an earthquake.

includes.label: PTSD and long-term mental health effects
includes.description: Earthquakes can have long-lasting effects on mental health, particularly among children and teenagers. One of the most common mental disorders resulting from earthquakes is Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), characterized by persistent intrusive memories, hyperarousal, avoidance of trauma-related cues, and negative changes in thinking and mood.

includes.label: Psychological/psychosocial support need
includes.description: Reports indicate psychological support for affected people is needed alongside short-term needs such as shelter, heating, household items, food items and health, as part of the response to major earthquakes.

includes.label: Overwhelmed medical/health capacity
includes.description: Reports from media and NGOs repeatedly focus on overwhelmed medical capacity, especially in Syria, with health facilities overwhelmed and a likely additional need for medical equipment and supplies; this affects the population's access to care and worsens health outcomes after the earthquake.

includes.label: Social science studies of health effects
includes.description: Post-earthquake social science data collection may investigate the health, social and economic effects of school and business closures, rates of injury and death among affected populations, and experiences of socially excluded or marginalized groups, as part of perishable data reconnaissance in the days to months after an event.
