nodes.label: Displacement and homelessness
nodes.description: Loss of shelter, homelessness and displacement of populations due to earthquake damage.

includes.label: Population displacement in damaged areas
includes.description: Rates of population displacement in moderately to heavily damaged geographic areas are a key social science data collection priority after earthquakes. In Türkiye, AFAD reported a total of 81,415 displaced people across 11 provinces, with 28,044 evacuated to other provinces due to the need for shelters. In Syria, more than 300,000 people were displaced in government-controlled areas, with 11,000 families left homeless as of 08 February due to building destruction.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Homelessness from housing loss
includes.description: When homes are destroyed or damaged by earthquake shaking, many people become homeless and require emergency shelter and housing solutions. In Syria, more than 5,100 buildings damaged and 2,000 destroyed left 11,000 families homeless; in Molise, entire town populations such as San Giuliano di Puglia (1,163 people) and Ripabottoni (673 people) were rendered homeless and assisted in tent camps.

includes.label: Reluctance to return home due to aftershocks
includes.description: The risk from aftershocks often leads people to settle outside their former homes, not wanting to move back in until the number of aftershocks decreases and the building has been assessed by structural engineers, prolonging displacement beyond the initial event.

includes.label: Evacuation to safer areas or other provinces
includes.description: Significant numbers of displaced people were evacuated outside the affected provinces toward other provinces due to the need for shelters; in Türkiye 28,044 people were evacuated outside affected provinces (23,437 by flights, 4,607 by road/rail), and Gendarmerie units created 23 accommodation/evacuation areas to collect people in need.

includes.label: Temporary shelter and tent camps
includes.description: Homeless populations are housed in temporary camps with tents and caravans; in Molise, large tent/caravan camps were set up at the entrance of towns such as Ripabottoni and San Giuliano, with some people sleeping in tents in their own courtyards or gardens, and a total of 1,728 tents/caravans provided to assist 19,560 people.

includes.label: Impacts on populations experiencing homelessness
includes.description: Social science research priorities include examining the experiences of socially excluded or marginalized populations, including people experiencing poverty, children, the elderly, people experiencing homelessness, and non-English speaking populations, in relation to earthquake impacts and displacement.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Shelter needs estimation models
includes.description: Data from past earthquakes show that the number of displaced people is almost an order of magnitude higher than the number of collapsed and severely destroyed buildings. Multi-criteria models estimate the number of displaced households and population needing temporary shelter based on building habitability (physical damage, loss of utilities, access to transport/services, weather), and social factors affecting desirability to evacuate (tenure, size, age, ethnicity, income, perception of security, distance to shelters).

includes.label: Displacement of refugee and vulnerable camp populations
includes.description: Earthquake displacement disproportionately affects already vulnerable populations such as refugees; UNRWA estimated that 90% of Palestinian refugees living in Lattakia camp, Al Nayrab camp, Ein al Tal camp, and Hama camp needed assistance as a result of the earthquake, compounding pre-existing displacement from the Syrian civil war.

includes.label: Earthquake displacement compounding conflict-driven displacement
includes.description: In Syria, the earthquake-induced displacement and homelessness compounded a pre-existing decade-long civil war crisis that had already caused extensive urban damage and population displacement, worsening the humanitarian situation for an already fragile and displaced population.

nodes.label: Service and access disruption
nodes.description: Disruption of transport, supply chains, logistics, access and overwhelmed health services.

includes.label: Transport and logistics disruption
includes.description: Increased air traffic and congested air space/reduced airport capacities cause delays for air relief; overland transport affected by population movements, damaged roads/train lines; supply chains disrupted; destruction/damage to ports, bridges and roads increases transportation costs and causes substantial shipment delays.

includes.label: Road blockage by rubble/debris
includes.description: Rubble can block roads and prevent access, hampering rescue efforts; destruction of roads, bridges and other infrastructure can make access and communication difficult; landslides and debris can also block roads or cause surface damage.

includes.label: Port and airport disruption
includes.description: Critical infrastructure such as ports and airports may become unusable due to earthquake and/or tsunami severity; a major Mediterranean port was partially damaged with containers toppled, followed by a major fire that brought all port operations to a halt, forcing freight liners to divert vessels to other ports and leaving unclear resumption timing.

includes.label: Power supply disruption
includes.description: Electrical infrastructure can be severely damaged; power cables ruptured or severed; approximately 30 substations belonging to Türkiye's Electricity Transmission Corporation suffered varying degrees of damage; blackouts reported in multiple locations; hospitals face power outages that could lead to death of patients in intensive care units.

includes.label: Telecommunications network disruption
includes.description: Telecommunications systems can be ruptured, severed or extensively damaged, hampering relief efforts and daily living; damaged communications systems isolate people and prevent coordination.

includes.label: Water supply and sanitation disruption
includes.description: Water and sanitation pipes can be ruptured or damaged; without proper sanitation and waste management the situation deteriorates rapidly increasing disease risk; rural areas facing water disruptions due to contamination of water station, reservoirs and tanks damaged in many areas; lack of clean water and toilets reported as risk factor for disease among survivors.

includes.label: Overwhelmed health services
includes.description: Local medical facilities are often overwhelmed by injured individuals requiring temporary field hospitals; at least 20 hospitals requested blood units, two hospitals in Idlib out of service, four hospitals damaged and evacuated in rebel-held areas; health facilities overwhelmed; reports continue to focus on overwhelmed medical capacity, especially in Syria, with need for additional medical equipment and supplies.

includes.label: Restricted humanitarian access
includes.description: Access to affected areas restricted due to damage and logistic issues; a key border crossing used for international aid temporarily closed due to damage; road connecting a major city to the aid hub reportedly inaccessible; transport feasibility assessments ongoing; access delayed by damage to road leading to the only approved/viable border crossing between two countries.

includes.label: Need for debris removal equipment
includes.description: Heavy machines (bulldozers, excavators, cranes), fuel and crews are indispensable for clearing roadways, providing access to blocked areas and enabling search and rescue; finding disposal areas is a challenge and debris should be recycled where possible; debris removal heavily needed for humanitarian access and in recovery phase for waste management.

includes.label: Disruption of hygiene services
includes.description: Normal hygiene services will be disrupted or non-functional after an earthquake, requiring responders and survivors to bring/acquire their own sanitary items such as wet wipes, toilet paper and sufficient clothing.

includes.label: Disrupted access to food and water
includes.description: Access to food and clean water in the disaster area may be disrupted; disrupted infrastructure may cut off access to food and clean water requiring distribution of rations, bottled water and purification equipment, as well as market support and cash incentives.

includes.label: Cascading impacts from lifeline interdependencies
includes.description: Post-earthquake investigations examine inter-system dependencies among different lifeline systems and recognize indirect and cascading impacts—positive or negative—of lifelines damage and disruption, as well as identification of elements critical to post-earthquake system functioning.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Time to restore lifeline services
includes.description: Post-earthquake investigations document restoration and repair activities for lifeline systems, including the time required to restore basic intended functions and service capabilities after the damage.

nodes.label: Social and security impacts
nodes.description: Protection risks, exploitation, abuse, crime and breakdown of law and order after disasters.

includes.label: Breakdown of law and order
includes.description: Chaos and confusion following earthquakes can lead to potential security risks, including increased crime rates due to overwhelmed law enforcement and a temporary breakdown of law and order.

includes.label: Rising crime and petty theft
includes.description: The risk of regular crime and petty theft may rise as people severely affected by the event may resort to negative coping mechanisms amid overwhelmed law enforcement.

includes.label: Exploitation, abuse and neglect of vulnerable groups
includes.description: A breakdown of social structures and services after earthquakes can result in increased risks of exploitation, abuse, and neglect for vulnerable groups; relief efforts must prioritize their unique needs to ensure safety and well-being.

includes.label: Heightened vulnerability of women and children
includes.description: Women and children often face heightened vulnerability and are disproportionately affected. Female-led households may have less access to resources, financial independence and decision-making power complicating recovery; children are particularly susceptible to physical harm and psychological trauma, may be orphaned, and face disrupted education and routines leading to long-term challenges.

includes.label: Children and women at risk of exploitation in crisis contexts
includes.description: In the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes, protection risks increased, with children and women from vulnerable families identified as being at risk of exploitation amid the humanitarian crisis.

includes.label: Protection risks for displaced populations
includes.description: Protection risks have increased for affected populations, particularly displaced people; response plans include measures to prevent and mitigate protection risks faced by the displaced population.

includes.label: Security measures for workplaces and rest places
includes.description: Due to security risks in the aftermath of earthquakes, both workplace and rest-place for responders need to be established with sufficient security measures in place.

includes.label: Socioeconomic vulnerability index including crime
includes.description: Integrated/holistic risk approaches attenuate or aggravate direct earthquake risk (average annual losses) according to a social vulnerability index derived from socioeconomic indicators such as crime, education, poverty, age or unemployment, reflecting earthquake resilience and expected recovery time of different regions.

includes.label: Post-earthquake social science data collection
includes.description: Social science investigations after earthquakes study human behavior, decision making, policy and socioeconomic relationships, including experiences of socially excluded or marginalized populations (poverty, children, elderly, homeless, non-English speakers), effects of school/business closures, and rates of population displacement; research involves collection of personally identifiable information requiring ethical safeguards.

nodes.label: Economic losses
nodes.description: Direct and indirect economic losses, costs of damage and financial impact of earthquakes.

includes.label: PAGER rapid economic loss alert
includes.description: USGS PAGER system issues colour-coded alerts for estimated economic losses soon after an earthquake (e.g. orange alert for the 2018 M7.1 Anchorage earthquake, with estimated losses under 1% of US GDP), informing decisions on regional/national response.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Economic loss as % of GDP
includes.description: Economic losses from major earthquakes are expressed as a share of national GDP; e.g. PAGER estimated up to 2% of Türkiye's GDP for the M7.8 event, while the cumulative 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes were later assessed at $103.6 billion, about 9% of Türkiye's 2023 GDP.

includes.label: Disproportionate damage cost in design
includes.description: Eurocode 8 performance requirement that structures must withstand frequent seismic actions without damage whose repair cost would be disproportionately high compared to the cost of the structure itself, linking design limit states to economic loss reduction.

includes.label: Economically unrecoverable structural damage
includes.description: Under rare seismic events a structure may remain standing (protecting life) but sustain substantial permanent damage, including permanent drifts, to the point that it becomes economically unrecoverable, i.e. repair cost exceeds replacement value.

includes.label: Business interruption / downtime loss
includes.description: Financial loss from the time needed to repair building damage (mobilisation time for assessment, contracting, debris clean-up, financing, plus repair time), causing loss of rental income or daily business revenue, and additional relocation/renting costs if the owner occupies the facility.

includes.label: Damage-to-loss models
includes.description: Models transforming structural/non-structural/content damage states into economic loss ratios: damage factors refer to the portion of construction cost needed to repair each damage state, including demolition and debris removal costs; content damage is assumed 100% loss when it occurs.

includes.label: Direct economic loss (repair cost)
includes.description: Seismic risk is expressed as direct economic loss, i.e. the cost of repairing buildings, estimated by combining exposure, hazard and vulnerability via fragility/vulnerability functions; expected loss ratios of 5%, 15%, 60% and 100% are assigned to damage states DS1–DS4 respectively.

includes.label: Average annual economic loss (AAEL)
includes.description: Risk metric representing the average amount of money that would be spent yearly to repair all buildings within a region if loss occurred regularly with the same amplitude; for 100 EU priority regions, seismic risk is estimated at 3.1 billion euro repair cost per year in residential buildings.

includes.label: Normalised average annual economic loss indicators
includes.description: Indicators normalising AAEL to building stock size (AAEL/bldg) or to total replacement cost (AAELR, expressed per mille), used to compare relative seismic economic risk across regions irrespective of absolute building counts or values.

includes.label: Economic benefit of seismic renovation
includes.description: Renovating building classes with a net economic benefit (prioritisation scenario A) reduces net annual economic loss by 78 million euro and fatalities by 28% (55 lives) across 47 EU regions; a more extensive scenario B yields smaller net economic loss reduction (12 million euro) but larger fatality reduction (36%, 71 lives).

includes.label: Loss exceedance curves
includes.description: Risk metric from probabilistic seismic risk analysis describing the probability of various levels of economic (and other) losses being exceeded; used to derive average annualized earthquake loss (AEL) and loss ratio (AELR) for comparing relative risk across regions.

includes.label: Debris generation from damaged/collapsed buildings
includes.description: Collapsed and severely damaged (uneconomical-to-repair) buildings generate large volumes of demolition debris with associated removal costs; the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes in Türkiye generated about 100 million tons of debris by May 2023.

includes.label: Earthquake insurance protection gap
includes.description: Earthquakes are among the hazards with the least insurance coverage worldwide; approximately 85% of earthquake-related economic losses globally since 2000 remain uninsured, with southern European countries such as Greece and Italy showing the highest protection gap scores due to high risk and low insurance penetration.

includes.label: Seismic risk transfer and insurance innovation
includes.description: Policy recommendation to explore insurance gaps at national level and develop new collaboration with the insurance sector for innovative products covering traditionally 'uninsurable' assets like cultural heritage, aiming to reduce major economic disruptions from earthquakes.

includes.label: Cumulative damage amplification from successive earthquakes
includes.description: Current loss estimation techniques cannot reliably account for cumulative damage when multiple major earthquakes strike the same area in short succession; buildings fragilised by a first event (e.g. M7.8) are expected to collapse under a subsequent event (e.g. M7.5), exacerbating overall economic losses beyond single-event estimates.

includes.label: Energy cost loss from inefficient buildings
includes.description: Beyond seismic repair costs, EU residential buildings consume annually more than 1900 TWh for heating at a cost of 180 billion euro; energy renovation combined with seismic retrofitting targets reduction of this recurring economic loss.

includes.label: Uncertainty in observed economic loss figures
includes.description: Total economic loss figures reported after an earthquake are difficult to define precisely and may not represent the same assets considered in exposure models, leading to high uncertainty when validating vulnerability models against observed losses from past events.

nodes.label: Environmental and hazardous material impact
nodes.description: Environmental effects including asbestos release and contamination following building damage.

includes.label: Asbestos fibre release from damaged buildings
includes.description: During and after an earthquake, obsolete buildings containing asbestos-containing materials (ACM) may be damaged depending on earthquake intensity and building fragility, releasing asbestos fibres into the atmosphere and creating a long-term health hazard. Measurements after the Great Hanshin earthquake showed asbestos fibre concentrations above acceptable limits where damaged ACM existed, with concentrations of 0.162 f/cc at 0h and 0.119 f/cc after 36h, still above the Korean acceptable limit of 0.01 f/cc.

includes.label: Increased atmospheric asbestos concentration
includes.description: Atmospheric monitoring after the Great Hanshin-Awaji earthquake showed an increase of asbestos concentration in the air by at least 1.5 times in the affected area; an estimated 3740 tonnes of sprayed-on asbestos existed in affected buildings prior to the earthquake and about 26.4 kg were released into the environment during the earthquake.

includes.label: Asbestos-related health effects after disaster
includes.description: Asbestos exposure following earthquake damage can cause long-term health hazards; after the Great Hanshin earthquake there was an increased number of pneumonia patients. Asbestos is linked to asbestos-related diseases including mesothelioma and lung cancer, and is a threat to the health of workers and occupants during repair of damaged buildings, as well as to residents exposed post-event.

includes.label: Asbestos waste mixed with demolition debris
includes.description: Post-earthquake building waste generates quantities of asbestos waste that must be separated from general demolition waste for disposal, reuse and recycling. This operation is challenging because asbestos waste is easily mixed with other wastes and is often not visible, increasing exposure risk during clean-up.

includes.label: Improper demolition/clean-up increasing asbestos exposure
includes.description: Improper demolition or improper clean-up of sites after an earthquake (or burnt asbestos material) can increase the local level of asbestos exposure, posing risks to workers and occupants during repair of damaged buildings.

includes.label: Seismic risk combined with asbestos presence creating exposure hotspots
includes.description: Estimated asbestos quantity in residential dwellings combined with seismic risk reveals EU regions where seismic activity may trigger increased asbestos exposure due to damage of the built environment. Regions with high seismic risk and high asbestos use are identified in southern Europe (notably Italy and Cyprus), with additional affected regions in Austria, Bulgaria, France, Germany, Slovenia and Hungary; central and northern Europe are less critical, while Ireland, Netherlands, Poland and Sweden are least affected.

includes.label: Natech hazardous material release triggered by earthquake
includes.description: Earthquakes act as powerful mechanisms of direct and indirect hazardous material (hazmat) releases from damaged buildings and facilities; such unintentional hazmat release triggered by natural disasters is defined as a natural-technologic (na-tech) event. Asbestos fibre release constitutes one example of such a secondary disaster in seismic-prone areas, occurring without affected communities being able to foresee its release, removal and clean-up.

nodes.label: Built environment vulnerability
nodes.description: Unreinforced or poorly built structures, lack of code enforcement and soft soils increasing damage potential.

includes.label: Unreinforced/poorly tied masonry walls
includes.description: Masonry infills and external walls without proper ties or connections between leaves suffered diagonal cracking, separation from beams/columns, and out-of-plane collapse. External walls built as two unconnected leaves, or resting only partially on beams, collapsed out-of-plane (e.g. a 20-25 m hospital facade wall with no lateral support). Poor quality materials combined with incorrect past restoration interventions led to extensive masonry damage, while steel ties and good conservation reduced vulnerability.

includes.label: Non-structural masonry envelope vulnerability
includes.description: Continuous masonry facades/envelopes behaved like free-standing walls independent of the frame structure but were not designed as such, leading to detrimental structural features observed in both old and new reinforced concrete buildings, such as masonry envelopes, beams only in one direction, and discontinued vertical elements.

includes.label: Lack of building code enforcement
includes.description: Enforcement and correct application of design codes is needed to gradually modernise local building traditions; previous national regulations were not properly classifying seismic zones and were not aligned with Eurocode prescriptions, contributing to vulnerability of the built stock. Code-uptake can be low even where codes exist, including in urban areas with formal settlements.

includes.label: Informal/non-engineered settlements
includes.description: Many small settlements fall into the 'informal settlement' typology, built without professional input or earthquake-resistant design, presenting structural vulnerability factors such as irregular shapes (generating weak points that accelerate collapse) and clustering of buildings with different floor heights causing pounding damage.

includes.label: Soft soil/unconsolidated ground amplification
includes.description: Terrain type affects seismic wave transmission: buildings on solid bedrock compliant with seismic codes are less likely to suffer damage, while those on unconsolidated rock and sediments may experience greater amplitude and duration of shaking, increasing damage potential. Local amplification due to site or topographic effects is a geotechnical priority linked to damage patterns.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Conflict-weakened buildings
includes.description: Many buildings in Syria had already been exposed to impacts from the conflict, reducing their ability to withstand the shock of an earthquake, which may be a decisive factor in collapse.

includes.label: Structural/horizontal-vertical irregularities
includes.description: Degree of building damage depends on horizontal and vertical irregularities of the building, the type and frequency of shaking waves, soil conditions, and building resilience; slightly/moderately damaged buildings may collapse during large aftershocks.

includes.label: Aging building stock without seismic provisions
includes.description: Most dwellings throughout European countries are in aging structures approaching or exceeding their conventional service lifespan, and most of the European building stock is vulnerable because it was designed without earthquake-resistance provisions or with only moderate-level seismic codes, particularly of concern in Southern and Eastern Europe with moderate-to-high seismicity.

includes.label: Vulnerable masonry/RC typologies in high seismic-hazard zones
includes.description: A significant share of masonry (~20%) and RC (~15%) buildings in Italy are located in high seismic hazard zones with severe climatic requirements; vulnerable masonry typologies are characterised by absence of connections among walls and floors, varying by construction period (pre-1945, pre-1971) and floor type (timber or RC floors), and also exhibit inadequate energy performance.

includes.label: High vulnerability of churches/heritage structures
includes.description: Churches resulted very vulnerable to seismic loads and experienced many local or global collapses; provisional supports were needed during pre-recovery and reconstruction phases to avoid further collapses and damage to frescos and artworks.

includes.label: Low uptake of earthquake insurance (risk retention)
includes.description: Owners of at-risk buildings often choose not to purchase earthquake insurance coverage due to low perception of earthquake risk, resulting in risk retention where individuals or entities bear the adverse consequences of an earthquake themselves.

includes.label: Non-structural component vulnerability
includes.description: Non-structural elements (architectural components such as partitions and ceilings; mechanical/electrical/plumbing components; furniture, fixtures and equipment) are distinct from structural elements and represent a further source of building vulnerability and damage/repair cost beyond structural failure.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

nodes.label: Exposure and timing factors
nodes.description: Population density, time of day, distance to epicentre and shallow depth increasing exposure to hazard.

includes.label: Distance to epicentre
includes.description: In most cases, the closer an area is to the earthquake epicentre, the more intense the shaking, increasing the likelihood of severe damage; the area closest to the epicentre is generally the hardest hit.

includes.label: Shallow focal depth
includes.description: Earthquakes closer to the surface cause more widespread damage because the shaking spreads over a larger area.

includes.label: Time of day of occurrence
includes.description: The time of day significantly affects earthquake severity as it governs how many people are in large buildings, at work or at school. Nighttime earthquakes can cause higher death tolls because more people are asleep inside vulnerable buildings that may collapse, and emergency response may be hindered by overnight mobilisation challenges.

includes.label: Population density
includes.description: Areas with higher population densities are at greater risk of extensive damage and loss of life in an earthquake, as more people and infrastructure are exposed; regions with high-density populations may experience more severe and widespread impacts from earthquakes of a given magnitude.

includes.label: Day/night/transit population distribution
includes.description: Population exposure varies by time of day: distribution between daytime (10:00-18:00), night-time (22:00-06:00) and transit-time (06:00-10:00, 18:00-22:00) is applied using national average percentages; since earthquakes can occur at any time, average 24-hour population is used in seismic risk calculations assuming equal probability across periods.

includes.label: Dynamic population exposure estimation
includes.description: Estimating population exposure for casualty models is challenging because it must account for daily commuting, weekly or seasonal population movements, and whether people are inside or near buildings at the time of the earthquake; datasets like the Global Human Settlement Layer only partially address this, given low geographic disaggregation and difficulty linking exposed individuals to specific building types.

includes.label: Proximity to epicentre concentrates damage
includes.description: Two major earthquakes (M7.8 and M7.5) with epicentres about 100 km apart produced largely overlapping areas of strong shaking, compounding damage to buildings already fragilized by the first event, illustrating how proximity and successive events amplify exposure.

includes.label: Local time of main shock
includes.description: The Molise earthquake struck at 11:32 am local time; the Türkiye earthquakes struck at 4:17 local time (1:17 UTC), illustrating how recorded local occurrence time is a factor in exposure of populations in buildings.

includes.label: Arrival time of hazard exposure
includes.description: For the dam breach scenario, exposed population figures are broken down by arrival time of floodwaters (e.g., 14,790 people exposed within 0-1 hr, up to 43,087 within 3-4 hrs), showing how time elapsed since the triggering earthquake affects exposure timing of downstream populations.

nodes.label: Social vulnerability
nodes.description: Poverty, gender, age, lack of awareness and pre-existing crises increasing susceptibility to harm.

includes.label: Pre-existing conflict/humanitarian crisis
includes.description: Decade-long civil war in Syria left infrastructure fragile and created a pre-existing very high severity humanitarian crisis (INFORM Severity 4.6/5), with 14.56 million people in need and 16.58 million displaced before the earthquake; this pre-existing crisis compounded earthquake impacts and complicated response, especially in rebel-controlled north-western Syria.

includes.label: Pre-existing IDP camp populations
includes.description: Nearly 1.7 million internally displaced people were already living in more than 1,400 camps under difficult conditions in rebel-held north-western Syria before the earthquake, increasing their vulnerability to the new disaster.

includes.label: Pre-existing aid dependency
includes.description: In north-western Syria, 90% of the population already relied on humanitarian aid to meet basic needs (food, non-food items, winter clothes, shelter) before the earthquake, making them especially susceptible to further disruption of assistance.

includes.label: Refugee population vulnerability
includes.description: UNRWA estimated that 90% of Palestinian refugees living in Lattakia, Al Nayrab, Ein al Tal and Hama camps needed assistance as a result of the earthquake, reflecting heightened vulnerability of refugee populations.

includes.label: Women and children vulnerability
includes.description: Women and children often face heightened vulnerability and are disproportionately affected by earthquakes; female-led households may have less access to resources, financial independence and decision-making power complicating recovery; children are particularly susceptible to physical harm and psychological trauma, may be orphaned, and face disrupted education and routines leading to long-term challenges.

includes.label: Protection risks: exploitation and abuse
includes.description: Breakdown of social structures and services after earthquakes increases risks of exploitation, abuse and neglect for vulnerable groups; relief efforts must prioritise their unique needs for safety and well-being. In Syria, children and women from vulnerable families were reported at risk of exploitation after the earthquake.

includes.label: Socioeconomic vulnerability index
includes.description: Socioeconomic vulnerability is derived from socioeconomic indicators such as crime, education, poverty, age and unemployment, and is used to aggravate or attenuate direct earthquake risk (e.g. average annual losses); regions with higher socioeconomic vulnerability are expected to need longer recovery times. In the EU, the top 100 regions with highest socioeconomic vulnerability accumulate 31% of fatalities and 25% of repair costs in residential buildings despite only 6% of energy consumption/cost, reflecting disproportionate social vulnerability in southern and eastern European regions.

includes.label: Impact on poverty reduction efforts
includes.description: Large annual earthquake economic losses (about one-fifth of global annual economic losses) and death tolls (more than 25,000 people per year) can seriously impact sustainable development, job creation and availability of funds for poverty reduction initiatives, indicating that poorer populations and economies are more vulnerable to being set back by earthquakes.

includes.label: Vulnerability from aging/non-seismic housing stock
includes.description: Most dwellings in European countries are aging structures approaching or exceeding conventional service lifespans, often built without seismic provisions or with only moderate-level seismic codes; this is of particular concern for Southern and Eastern European nations with moderate to high seismicity, with substantial implications for large portions of the population who are socially vulnerable to associated losses.

includes.label: Lack of awareness and shelter suitability studies
includes.description: Studies such as suitability analysis of shelter spaces (e.g. Kathmandu) and earthquake risk awareness campaigns have been developed to address the general lack of public knowledge and preparedness that increases social vulnerability to earthquake impacts.

nodes.label: Environmental conditions
nodes.description: Weather, climate and seasonal conditions such as cold, heat or rainy season that aggravate impacts.

includes.label: Cold climate / winter conditions
includes.description: In the event of an earthquake during winter in cold climates, survivors are at high risk of experiencing hypothermia, frostbite and other illnesses caused by prolonged exposure to damp and cold weather. Bad weather can also hinder rescue efforts and make response much harder.

includes.label: Increased fire risk from indoor heating
includes.description: During cold weather there is a higher likelihood that stoves and fires are burning inside houses that have collapsed, significantly increasing the chances of fires after the earthquake.

includes.label: Hot climate conditions
includes.description: When earthquakes occur in hot climates, the lack of water makes it harder for people trapped in rubble to survive.

includes.label: Local climatic conditions affecting heating needs
includes.description: Local climatic conditions, represented by heating degree days (HDDs) derived from outside air temperature measurements, determine space heating energy requirements of residential buildings; these are combined with seismic vulnerability in building renovation prioritisation studies.

includes.label: Concurrent drought conditions
includes.description: Following the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes, both countries were under severe drought warning conditions (Copernicus European Drought Observatory), with severe lack of precipitation and drier-than-normal soil moisture, compounding earthquake impacts on water availability for agriculture and energy.

includes.label: Seasonal transition from dry heat to monsoon rains
includes.description: In Myanmar, warm to hot conditions were expected for the coming months, peaking in the Central Dry Zone in April, with the monsoon starting in May bringing heavy rain to coastal and hilly areas, affecting ongoing disaster response.

nodes.label: Critical infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: Structural and systemic weaknesses of critical, non-nuclear infrastructure to seismic and cascading hazards.

includes.label: Limited exposure and vulnerability databases
includes.description: Availability of open exposure and vulnerability databases is quite limited; existing global databases (e.g. GEM, USGS PAGER) have varying levels of detail by country, and there is a predominance of fragility over vulnerability functions and damage-to-loss models, with a notable lack of vulnerability functions for many developing countries due to scarce past-event loss data and the difficulty of modelling non-engineered buildings.

includes.label: Cascading effects on critical infrastructure
includes.description: Vulnerability assessment of critical infrastructures to natural hazards must primarily target cascading effects the earthquake may induce, as these are generally the main loss drivers rather than direct damage alone (e.g. industrial accidents triggered by facility damage).

includes.label: Single-site high-consequence facility vulnerability
includes.description: Class A critical infrastructures are individual, single-site facilities (e.g. power plants, oil refineries, dams) where hazard is assessed at a point-like location but vulnerability must account for systems capable of domino and cascading effects affecting surrounding communities; direct damage is typically a negligible fraction of loss while triggered effects (e.g. an industrial accident) generate the main loss.

includes.label: Distributed lifeline network vulnerability
includes.description: Class B critical infrastructures are spatially-distributed systems (e.g. utility distribution networks, gas pipelines, ports) needing hazard and vulnerability assessment that reflects their systemic, interconnected nature and non-point-like spatial configuration; local failure can cause lifeline interruption for large served communities, with downtime usually the main cause of loss, though triggered accidents (e.g. hazardous material release in gas networks) can also occur.

includes.label: Building portfolio accumulated loss vulnerability
includes.description: Class C critical infrastructures are typified by building portfolios (e.g. industrial districts) where individual hazardous events may trigger accumulated losses due to multiple local failures and business downtime; contemporaneous losses across a portfolio can be large enough that the portfolio itself must be treated as critical infrastructure.

includes.label: Infrastructure interdependencies
includes.description: Different critical infrastructure components and systems exhibit numerous dependencies (geographic, physical, restoration, sequential, information, general) with the most found in hydrocarbon pipeline systems, harbour facilities and gas storage/distribution networks (up to 110, 102 and 88 dependencies respectively); geographic and physical dependencies are the most common, and a 'dependency index' shows some assets (e.g. industrial districts) are more interdependent than others, affecting cascading vulnerability during earthquakes.

includes.label: Pipeline network seismic vulnerability
includes.description: Major hydrocarbon and gas pipeline networks are vulnerable to seismic ground shaking and permanent ground deformation; performance is assessed via fragility curves for pipelines and stations using the SYNER-G 'Shakefields' method to generate spatially-correlated seismic intensity maps across network nodes and branches (modelled as a graph of nodes and links), with repair rates (number of pipe repairs per unit length) as a key performance measure.

includes.label: Port infrastructure seismic vulnerability
includes.description: Port infrastructures (waterfront structures, cranes, liquid storage facilities) are vulnerable to seismic ground shaking and liquefaction; existing fragility functions for waterfront structures and cranes have been reviewed and new analytical fragility curves developed for buildings and container crane infrastructures, with performance assessed via connectivity and capacity analyses, accounting for interactions among port elements and simulated port operations.

includes.label: Precast industrial warehouse vulnerability
includes.description: Precast concrete warehouse buildings typical of European industrial districts have demonstrated high levels of damage in past earthquakes; damage can affect the structural system, non-structural components (e.g. external cladding) and building contents, since roof systems made of precast elements do not behave as a rigid diaphragm during a seismic event, leading to direct economic losses and business interruption.

includes.label: Non-structural components and contents fragility
includes.description: Non-structural components and building contents within critical facilities have fragility functions based on peak floor acceleration (approximated by peak ground acceleration for single-storey buildings); contents restraint quality (poor, moderate, superior) affects vulnerability, and damage typically results in full replacement, with 100% damage factor assumed if the structure collapses.

includes.label: Business interruption and downtime
includes.description: Damage to critical infrastructure and industrial buildings leads to business interruption or downtime, defined as the time needed to repair building damage, comprising mobilisation time and repair time; this downtime is a major driver of indirect economic losses in distributed lifeline systems where local failure causes serviceability or connectivity loss for served communities.

includes.label: Lack of multi-hazard and multi-event vulnerability models
includes.description: Vulnerability and risk assessment models for critical infrastructure are mostly lacking for hazards other than seismic, and models to address multi-event or multi-hazard loss assessment (e.g. structural deterioration from repeated shocks/aftershocks) are far from being fully developed, even though the research pathway is clear.

includes.label: Large dam seismic vulnerability
includes.description: Large dams are treated as Class A single-site high-consequence critical infrastructure requiring vulnerability models capable of capturing cascading and domino effects; dams show significant numbers of interdependencies (64 identified in one case study) with other systems, relevant to stress-testing against seismic hazard.

nodes.label: Energy inefficiency and building stock vulnerability
nodes.description: Combination of poor energy performance and seismic weakness in existing building stock.

includes.label: Combined energy inefficiency and seismic weakness
includes.description: A large proportion of the EU building stock is both energy-inefficient and structurally vulnerable due to old age; the majority of buildings in seismic regions are vulnerable to earthquakes and are commonly also energy inefficient, meaning the two weaknesses co-occur in the same existing building stock.

includes.label: EU buildings in moderate seismic hazard zones
includes.description: 30% of European buildings are located in areas of moderate seismic hazard where the design peak ground acceleration (PGA) is at least 0.1g, exposing a significant share of the (often energy-inefficient) building stock to seismic risk.

includes.label: Building stock energy consumption and emissions
includes.description: The European building stock is responsible for 40% of energy consumption and 36% of CO2 emissions in the EU, making it the single largest energy consumer in Europe; this poor energy performance is combined with seismic vulnerability in many regions.

includes.label: Pre-1945/pre-1971 masonry building typologies
includes.description: Masonry building typologies without connections among walls and floors, built before 1945 or 1971, were identified (based on post-earthquake damage/safety assessment forms, e.g. after the Emilia earthquake) as most vulnerable to earthquake damage; they also exhibit inadequate energy performance, since envelope thermal properties do not comply with current Italian energy efficiency regulations (based on TABULA database data).

includes.label: Pre/post-1971 RC frame typologies needing seismic renovation
includes.description: RC frame structures designed without seismic requirements were found to be the most widespread RC structural typology in Italy; two typologies (pre-1971 and post-1971, differing in material properties, floor area, and number of storeys) were identified as most needing seismic renovation, reflecting combined structural and energy vulnerability.

includes.label: Asbestos presence combined with seismic risk
includes.description: Certain EU regions combine asbestos presence in buildings with seismic risk; fostering deep building renovation in these regions could bring energy and emission savings while also reducing seismic risk (e.g. Greece, Italy) and asbestos exposure (e.g. Belgium, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania).

includes.label: Regions combining seismic risk, poor energy performance and socioeconomic vulnerability
includes.description: Integrated indicators identify EU regions, mainly in south-eastern Europe (e.g. Romania, Greece, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bulgaria), where high seismic risk, high energy consumption/cost, and socioeconomic vulnerability overlap; about 100 such priority regions account for roughly 10% of EU energy consumption/cost, 61% of fatalities, and 49% of repair cost from seismic events.

includes.label: Greater cost-effectiveness of integrated vs. separate retrofitting
includes.description: Integrating energy and seismic retrofitting of buildings is reported as more cost-effective than energy retrofitting alone in seismic regions of Europe; integrated renovation saves more lives, minimises disturbance to occupants and services, reduces initial costs, optimises material use and reduces demolition waste compared to separate seismic or energy-only interventions.

includes.label: Aging building stock vulnerability
includes.description: A large proportion of the EU building stock presents structural vulnerabilities due to its old age, compounding its poor energy performance and increasing susceptibility to seismic damage.

nodes.label: Life-saving needs
nodes.description: Needs for search and rescue and emergency medical care in the immediate aftermath.

includes.label: Urban search and rescue (USAR) teams
includes.description: Specialized INSARAG-certified USAR teams (heavy, medium, light, canine K-9) are among the first responders deployed to detect and extract survivors trapped in collapsed buildings; speed is critical and teams are deployed as quickly as possible. In Türkiye, 31+ UCPM USAR teams plus dozens of other national teams were deployed/mobilising; 45 people were rescued by UCPM-deployed teams by 9 February. In Myanmar, 23 international USAR teams from nine countries were deployed, with national teams also mobilised. In Syria, only about 5% of needed search and rescue operations were being covered.

includes.label: Critical rescue window for trapped survivors
includes.description: Structural collapses generate trapped victims who may survive for several days under ideal conditions (food, water, temperate climate), but 85-95% of persons rescued alive from collapsed buildings are rescued in the first 24-48 hours after an earthquake, underscoring the urgency of rapid search and rescue.

includes.label: Emergency medical care for injured
includes.description: Local medical facilities are often overwhelmed by injured individuals; most injuries are minor cuts and bruises, followed by simple fractures, and a minority with severe multiple fractures and internal injuries requiring surgery and intensive treatment for crush syndrome. Within 3-5 days most injured arrive at medical facilities, in two waves (local then referred cases). Temporary field hospitals with emergency medical personnel, supplies and equipment are essential.

includes.label: Crush syndrome treatment
includes.description: A minority of earthquake-injured persons present multiple severe fractures and internal injuries requiring surgery and intensive treatment for crush syndrome, a life-threatening condition requiring specialized medical care.

includes.label: Field hospitals and Emergency Medical Teams
includes.description: Temporary field hospitals equipped with emergency medical personnel, supplies and equipment are essential for treating overwhelming numbers of injured. In Türkiye, UCPM mobilised EMT1, EMT2 and medical teams from several countries; in Myanmar, EMTs from India, Japan, Russia, Canada, Philippines and USA were deployed or mobilising to provide medical assistance alongside search and rescue.

includes.label: Medical supplies, equipment and blood units
includes.description: Urgent need for medical equipment, medicines, trauma and emergency surgical kits, ambulances, fuel for hospitals, and blood units; at least 20 hospitals in Syria requested blood units, and hospitals were overwhelmed or out of service, requiring additional medical equipment and supplies.

includes.label: Medical evacuation transport
includes.description: Specialized transportation means, such as a C130 transport aircraft offered by the Netherlands and accepted by Türkiye, were mobilised under the UCPM specifically for medical evacuations of casualties.

includes.label: Rapid building safety assessment
includes.description: UNDP identified rapid building safety assessment as a short-term (0-3 month) priority alongside support to local-level emergency coordination, to determine whether damaged structures are safe before people re-enter or to guide rescue operations.

includes.label: Social media-based identification of help requests
includes.description: JRC developed the SMDRM AI deep learning tool to automatically classify social media messages and images; for the Türkiye-Syria earthquake it processed over 1 million user-generated messages, filtering and georeferencing those requesting help to quickly support search and rescue operations.

nodes.label: Basic needs
nodes.description: Needs for shelter, food, water, sanitation and hygiene among affected populations.

includes.label: Emergency shelter and housing
includes.description: When homes are destroyed, many people become homeless and require emergency shelter and housing solutions. Shelter supplies such as tents, cots, blankets and essential living items are immediate needs; aftershock fear leads people to settle outside former homes until structural assessment is done. Evacuation shelters offering temporary housing, food/water, hygiene services and medical aid should be prioritised. In Syria/Türkiye, shelter, tents, blankets and winter clothes were urgently needed; millions of children needed shelter.

includes.label: Food and water distribution
includes.description: Disrupted infrastructure may cut off access to food and clean water. Distributing food rations, bottled water and purification equipment helps stabilize supplies; market support and cash incentives should be considered. In north-western Syria 90% of people already relied on aid for food and non-food items; emergency food and nutrition assistance needed for affected populations in Türkiye and Syria.

includes.label: WASH and hygiene services
includes.description: Water supply treatment and reconstruction of water supply and drainage/sewer systems is vital; without proper sanitation and waste management the situation deteriorates rapidly, increasing communicable disease risk. Distribution of hygiene items, latrines and hygiene promotion should be prioritised. In Syria, water stations, reservoirs and tanks were damaged, rural Aleppo faced water disruptions from contamination, and water trucking, rehabilitation of water structures and hygiene assistance were identified as WASH priorities amid an ongoing cholera outbreak.

includes.label: Non-food items and hygiene kits
includes.description: Critical non-food items (NFIs) such as blankets, cooking items, first aid kits and hygiene items are needed by affected populations alongside food and shelter. UNDP identified 'Critical NFIs Support' as a short-term (0-3 month) response priority after the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes.

includes.label: Estimating temporary shelter demand
includes.description: Multi-criteria models estimate the number of displaced households, population needing temporary shelter and required shelter supplies (food and water), based on building habitability (physical damage, loss of utilities, access to transport and services, weather conditions) and social factors affecting desirability to evacuate (tenure, household size, age, income, employment, perception of security, distance to shelters).

includes.label: Cash and market-based assistance
includes.description: Market support and cash incentives should be considered as part of food/water response. UNDP identified 'Multi-purpose Cash Assistance' as a short-term priority and 'Cash for shelter assistance' as a mid-term recovery intervention following the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes.

includes.label: Pre-existing dependence on aid for basic needs
includes.description: In contexts with pre-existing humanitarian crises (e.g. north-western Syria), 90% of the population already relied on humanitarian aid to meet basic needs including food and non-food items, winter clothes, shelters, tents and blankets even before the earthquake, compounding post-earthquake basic needs gaps.

includes.label: Shelter and WASH needs assessments
includes.description: Inter-agency and cluster-specific assessments including nutrition, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), and building integrity were conducted in affected governorates to identify basic needs gaps and guide humanitarian response targeting.

includes.label: Personal emergency supply kit
includes.description: Individuals are advised to keep a grab bag with essential items, identification documents, flashlight, appropriate clothing and a whistle near resting places in case of nighttime evacuation, reflecting basic personal preparedness for shelter/safety needs during aftershocks.

nodes.label: Services and access needs
nodes.description: Needs for restoring power, communications, logistics, transport, debris removal and structural safety assessment.

includes.label: Structural safety assessment need
includes.description: No infrastructure can be assumed safe after an earthquake without assessment by certified structural engineers; post-earthquake safety evaluations rate buildings (e.g. Red/Yellow/Green Tag, ATC 20-1 field manual) to determine suitability for immediate occupancy; USAR teams may have capacity to carry out such assessments; rapid building safety assessment is identified as a short-term priority.

includes.label: Power restoration need
includes.description: Electrical infrastructure can be severely damaged by earthquakes; hospitals may face power outages that can lead to death of ICU patients; bringing in generators, repair crews and equipment, and coordinating repairs is key to restoring power access.

includes.label: Communications network restoration
includes.description: Damaged communications systems isolate people and prevent coordination; rapid deployment of temporary cell towers, satellite phones, radios and internet connectivity aids rescue coordination, supports situational awareness and reconnects affected populations.

includes.label: Logistics and transport access needs
includes.description: Increased air traffic, congested airspace and reduced airport capacity cause delays affecting all relief transported by air; overland transport affected by population movements, damaged roads/train lines; destruction or damage to ports, bridges and roads increases transport costs and causes shipment delays; temporary solutions needed to ferry aid and allow people to leave impacted zones; supply chains disrupted.

includes.label: Debris removal need
includes.description: Rubble can block roads and prevent access; heavy construction equipment (bulldozers, excavators, cranes) and crews are indispensable for clearing roadways, providing access to blocked areas, and enabling search and rescue; finding disposal areas for rubble is a challenge and debris should be recycled where possible; heavy machines, fuel and equipment for debris removal identified as a priority need for humanitarian access, and debris removal/waste management continues into the recovery phase.

includes.label: Lifeline systems restoration need
includes.description: Lifelines (communications, electric power, natural gas and liquid fuels, potable water, solid waste management, stormwater drainage, transportation, wastewater) are fundamental services essential to health, safety and socio-economic security; earthquakes can damage and disrupt lifeline functioning, causing cascading effects on resource flows and significant social/economic impacts at regional, national and global scale; post-earthquake investigations document direct physical and operational damage, disruption and resilience of lifeline networks.

includes.label: Water and sanitation infrastructure restoration
includes.description: Reconstruction of water supply systems and drainage/sewer systems is vital after disruption; without proper sanitation and waste management, survivor conditions deteriorate rapidly and increase the risk of communicable diseases.

includes.label: Rapid damage and debris mapping need
includes.description: Satellite-based Copernicus Risk & Recovery Mapping can detect the presence and volume of debris and monitor the removal and reconstruction process; JRC analyses estimate numbers of damaged buildings and assess feasibility of rubble detection in affected cities to inform response and recovery.

includes.label: Debris removal for humanitarian access
includes.description: Identified as a short-term (0-3 month) response priority: debris removal is needed specifically to restore humanitarian access to affected areas, alongside rapid building safety assessment, critical NFI support, psychosocial support and cash assistance.

includes.label: Debris removal and waste management for recovery
includes.description: In the mid-term (3-18 months), response interventions focus on debris removal and waste management for recovery, alongside rehabilitation of critical basic and social infrastructure and local markets.

includes.label: Rehabilitation of critical infrastructure need
includes.description: Mid-term recovery interventions include rehabilitation of critical basic and social infrastructure and rehabilitation of local markets and small businesses for livelihood recovery.

nodes.label: Protection and psychosocial needs
nodes.description: Needs for protection of vulnerable groups and psychosocial support for affected populations.

includes.label: Protection risks for vulnerable groups
includes.description: Emergency situations exacerbate existing inequalities and lead to a rise in human rights and protection concerns; breakdown of social structures and services increases risks of exploitation, abuse and neglect for vulnerable groups; relief efforts must prioritize their unique needs to ensure safety and well-being. Protection risks increased in Syria and Türkiye after the 2023 earthquakes, with children and women from vulnerable families at risk of exploitation and unexploded ordnances present in many areas.

includes.label: Centrality of protection in response
includes.description: Special consideration should be given to known protection risks in the context, referencing the broader principle of centrality of protection and quality response in humanitarian operations after earthquakes.

includes.label: Exploitation risk for displaced populations
includes.description: Children and women from vulnerable families, including displaced populations, are identified as at risk of exploitation following earthquakes; the UNDP response plan explicitly lists protection activities for preventing and mitigating risks faced by displaced populations.

includes.label: Psychosocial/mental health support need
includes.description: Psychological support and mental health services are needed for affected populations; cited as a short-term UNDP priority (Psychosocial Support) and noted as needed in the Turkiye flash appeal ('Physiological support for the affected people is also needed'); mental health services also listed under WASH-related humanitarian needs in Syria.

includes.label: Protection as humanitarian response sector
includes.description: Protection is identified as one of the main immediate humanitarian needs/sectors after the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes, focused on preventing and mitigating protection risks, especially for the displaced population; it is also included among sectors supported by the UN Flash Appeal for Türkiye (food security, protection, education, water and shelter).

includes.label: Socioeconomic vulnerability affecting recovery
includes.description: Socioeconomic vulnerability of exposed populations (e.g., human development, social progress, and EU2020 indices) complements physical vulnerability and affects populations' ability to access basic needs (shelter, water/sanitation, security, nutrition and basic medical care) and recover after an earthquake.

nodes.label: Information and assessment needs
nodes.description: Needs for rapid damage assessment, situational awareness and scientific information to guide response.

includes.label: Post-earthquake investigation coordination
includes.description: Formal mechanisms (e.g. NEHRP Plan, PCWG-EIC, Technical Clearinghouse) to coordinate post-earthquake scientific investigations: appointing an Earthquake Investigation Committee, categorizing event significance levels, coordinating with state/partner agencies, and enabling real-time field communication between investigators through briefings and on-site presence.

includes.label: Perishable data collection
includes.description: Need to rapidly gather time-sensitive field observations of earthquake effects (direct, indirect and cascading impacts including landslides, liquefaction, fire-following, tsunamis) using geoscience, engineering and social science disciplines, including new sources such as social media, citizen science and satellite imagery, before they are lost; all observations should be timestamped and geotagged, and technical investigation must not interfere with emergency response.

includes.label: Technical clearinghouse for field data
includes.description: Establishment of a Technical Clearinghouse enabling real-time field communication between investigators through designated channels, organized briefings and on-site presence, historically opened for more than 30 domestic and international earthquakes over two decades, informing both emergency response and long-term recovery.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Rapid information dissemination to public/authorities
includes.description: Immediate alerts to the public and government agencies at all levels about the occurrence and scope of an earthquake, followed by information on types and concentrations of observed damage, improving effectiveness of emergency responses and long-term recovery.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Rapid impact estimation systems
includes.description: Automated systems (e.g. GDACS) issuing RED notifications within minutes of an earthquake using shakemaps, repeatedly updated as shaking intensity data is refined, sent to tens of thousands of users to inform emergency response.

includes.label: Collaborative global impact modelling
includes.description: Collaboration between agencies (e.g. GEM, JRC, ERCC) to produce impact estimations for fatalities, injuries, building damage and economic damage, informing humanitarian decision-making, satellite acquisition planning, deployment of international responders and quantification of response funding needs.

includes.label: Satellite rapid mapping for damage assessment
includes.description: Activation of satellite emergency mapping services (e.g. Copernicus EMS) to acquire very-high-resolution optical imagery over areas of interest near epicentres, supporting damage assessment; results published as multiple products viewable on activation portals within days of the event.

includes.label: Debris volume quantification and monitoring
includes.description: Need for methodology and satellite-based services (e.g. Copernicus Risk & Recovery Mapping) to detect and quantify huge volumes of debris in affected areas, monitor removal process and reconstruction phase, as debris contributes to insecurity, displacement and service interruption.

includes.label: Remote-sensing building damage classification
includes.description: Multi-temporal damage assessments using high-resolution satellite imagery and manual visual analysis to classify building damage into four classes (slight, moderate, severe, destroyed/razed to ground), supporting Post-Disaster Needs Assessment preparation.

includes.label: Destroyed building count estimation
includes.description: Quantitative monitoring of destroyed buildings using crowdsourced data (e.g. HOTOSM) combined with satellite-derived building block delineation and population grids, to characterise extent of damage per city/block for recovery planning.

includes.label: Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA)
includes.description: Collective, multi-agency process (EU, World Bank, UN Development Group) to assess reconstruction and rehabilitation needs and estimate overall costs after an earthquake, combining humanitarian needs assessment, damage/loss assessment and development of a comprehensive recovery plan; notably longer timeline than preliminary rapid assessments.

includes.label: Rapid early recovery evaluation
includes.description: Need for preliminary needs assessments and rapid early recovery evaluations to provide an evidence basis for donor conferences and interlocutions, produced faster than complete PDNA, covering building damage quantification and rubble detection.

includes.label: Coordinated needs assessment cell
includes.description: Multi-partner Assessment & Analysis (A&A) Cell chaired by UN-OCHA, bringing together remote sensing, secondary data, primary data collection, GIS and humanitarian needs analysis expertise (e.g. ACAPS, ERCC/JRC, IFRC, MapAction, UNDAC, IMPACT/REACH, HDX, IMMAP, Kobo, Logs Cluster, UNOSAT) to agree common strategy for timely decision-support analysis in the first phase of sudden-onset response.

includes.label: In-depth post-disaster impact assessment
includes.description: Mid-term (3-18 months) priority for conducting detailed post-disaster impact assessment informing rehabilitation of critical infrastructure, local markets and livelihood recovery planning.

includes.label: Fatality and injury count monitoring
includes.description: Tracking and reporting the evolving number of fatalities and injured persons over hours/days after an earthquake, drawing on media and national authority bulletins, to inform response planning.

includes.label: Mis/disinformation monitoring
includes.description: Analysis to detect and summarise narratives from unverified sources spreading mis/disinformation about an earthquake disaster, for limited distribution within civil protection mechanisms to counter false narratives affecting response.

includes.label: Epidemic intelligence monitoring
includes.description: Continuous monitoring of health-related news and open-source epidemic intelligence systems (e.g. EIOS) for new or worsened disease outbreaks (e.g. cholera) in earthquake-affected areas.

includes.label: Social media help-request detection
includes.description: Monitoring social media to identify messages requesting help after an earthquake; georeferencing filtered, location-tagged messages and quickly sharing them to support search and rescue operations.

includes.label: Seismic risk renovation impact assessment
includes.description: Integrated analysis framework assessing regional impacts and cost-benefit of building renovation scenarios across the EU, quantifying reductions in economic loss, loss of life and energy consumption, and economic feasibility, to inform prioritisation of prevention investment.

includes.label: National seismic risk quantification
includes.description: Estimation of annual seismic risk (e.g. 197 fatalities and €3.1 billion repair cost per year in residential buildings for priority regions) and of the impact of renovation scenarios (reducing fatalities by 28-36% and net economic loss) to guide national risk-informed prioritisation.

nodes.label: Building codes and standards
nodes.description: Design codes, standards such as Eurocode 8 and regulatory frameworks for seismic-resistant construction.

includes.label: Eurocode 8 seismic design standard
includes.description: EN 1998 (Eurocode 8) is the European standard 'Design of structures for earthquake resistance', applying to design and construction of buildings and civil engineering works in seismic regions; it is complementary to other Eurocodes (EN1990-EN1997, EN1999) and is composed of 6 parts (general rules/buildings, bridges, assessment and retrofitting, silos/tanks/pipelines, foundations/geotechnical, towers/masts/chimneys). It aims to ensure human lives are protected, damage is limited and structures important for civil protection remain operational in the event of earthquakes.

includes.label: No-collapse and damage-limitation requirements
includes.description: Eurocode 8 (EN 1998-1) establishes two explicit performance requirements for seismic design: a no-collapse requirement (structure withstands the design seismic action without local or global collapse, retaining structural integrity and residual load-bearing capacity) and a damage-limitation requirement (structure withstands a more frequent seismic action without damage or associated use limitations whose repair costs would be disproportionate).

includes.label: Nationally determined parameters
includes.description: Eurocodes allow small national variations through Nationally Determined Parameters, giving a recommended value or procedure for each, while National Authorities retain control over safety and economic consequences of structural design in their countries; most countries have adopted recommended values.

includes.label: Seismic micro-zonation
includes.description: Italian Law 64 introduced for the first time seismic micro-zonation, attempting to account for local site effects of earthquakes in design codes.

includes.label: Seismic design spectra in codes
includes.description: Following Law 64, the 1975 Italian decree introduced seismic design spectra with peak ground acceleration lower than expected for strong events because hysteretic behaviour of structures was taken into account; for the first time seismic resistance was required also for masonry buildings.

includes.label: Post-earthquake code updates
includes.description: After major Italian earthquakes (Friuli 1976, Irpinia 1980) new regional/national codes on seismic behaviour of structures were issued, focusing on retrofitting criteria and giving first rules to calculate and verify resistance of masonry to seismic loads, as well as describing retrofitting systems and measures to reduce seismic effects and increase structural resistance.

includes.label: Prestressed tie prescription for masonry
includes.description: A 1975 Italian decree prescribed the use of pre-stressed ties as a retrofitting/strengthening system for masonry, with prestressing not exceeding 50% of maximum allowable steel stress and anchoring distributing stress on the masonry; despite this, lack of ties remains a common cause of collapse of old masonry structures in recent seismic events.

includes.label: Seismic design code level classification
includes.description: A classification system (CDN–No, CDL–Low, CDM–Moderate, CDH–High) assigns a seismic design code level to building classes based on year of construction and evolution of codes in each EU Member State, reflecting whether buildings were designed with no seismic provisions, allowable stress method, limit state method, or capacity design with target ductility.

includes.label: Lateral force coefficient (k)
includes.description: For RC and mixed masonry-RC building classes, an additional attribute, the lateral force coefficient k (seismic design shear normalised to building weight), is calculated by combining a seismic coefficient, structural coefficient, importance coefficient and dynamic coefficient, used to characterise the level of seismic design applied historically across EU countries.

includes.label: Building code enforcement and grants
includes.description: FEMA is mandated to operate grant programs enabling States to update building, land-use planning and zoning codes/ordinances to enhance seismic safety, purchase instrumentation, conduct seismic safety inspections of critical structures and lifelines, and support multi-State cooperative agreements and demonstration projects.

includes.label: Dissemination of seismic design guidance
includes.description: FEMA, with NIST, other federal agencies and private sector groups, uses research results to support preparation, maintenance and wide dissemination of seismic-resistant design guidance and information on building codes, standards and practices for new and existing buildings and lifeline infrastructure, and aids development of performance-based design guidelines and cost-effective model codes.

includes.label: Seismic hazard model informing design codes
includes.description: The 2020 European Seismic Hazard Model (ESHM20) provides updated probabilistic hazard assessment across the Euro-Mediterranean region and informs the provisions of seismic design codes; National Annexes to Eurocode 8 contain country-specific reference peak ground acceleration maps based on such seismic hazard studies, using a 475-year reference return period, though developed at different times with different models.

includes.label: Combined seismic-energy building renovation programmes
includes.description: Several EU countries have introduced legal/regulatory measures combining energy efficiency with seismic (and sometimes fire) safety requirements for building renovation, e.g. Bulgaria's 2015 national programme, Italy's Ecosisma bonus/Superbonus, Portugal's law addressing energy efficiency, seismic and fire safety, Romania's apartment building programme extended to include seismic evaluation, and Slovenia's Building Cards instrument; recognised also in national long-term renovation strategies and recovery and resilience plans of several Member States.

includes.label: Code provisions for non-structural elements
includes.description: Building codes include design provisions aimed at making non-structural elements resistant to seismic loads, with literature providing guidelines and recommendations for practical measures to reduce or prevent damage to non-structural elements, enhancing occupant safety and ensuring functionality and business continuity.

includes.label: Global seismic building code resources
includes.description: FEMA and the International Association of Earthquake Engineering (IAEE) provide online resources on Seismic Building Codes, and the Global Earthquake Model (GEM) Foundation has produced a global map of earthquake hazard and risk, with underlying national/regional models often developed in collaboration with national governments to provide a scientific basis for development of seismic design codes.

nodes.label: Retrofitting and renovation
nodes.description: Structural retrofitting, strengthening and combined seismic-energy renovation techniques for existing buildings.

includes.label: RC infilling of existing frames
includes.description: Converting selected bays of multi-storey multi-bay RC frame buildings into new structural walls by infilling with reinforced concrete. Described as the most effective and economic method for retrofitting RC buildings, especially those with soft storeys. Full-scale tests at ELSA (SERFIN project) on a four-storey, three-bay frame showed five times higher resistance to earthquake loads compared to typical 1970s Cyprus construction; the structure sustained an earthquake of 0.25g without significant damage, demonstrating it as a viable method to strengthen ductility- and strength-deficient structures.

includes.label: FRP strengthening and jacketing
includes.description: Use of fibre-reinforced polymers (FRP) and concrete jacketing of RC beams and columns to increase flexural and shear strength and deformation capacity, applied as a local retrofitting measure when a building already has acceptable lateral strength and stiffness. Noted as one of the most frequently researched retrofitting types, fully covered by Eurocode 8 – Part 3, and used in SERFIN tests where three-sided CFRP wraps protected wall-bounding columns at ground floor and prevented lap-splice failure.
