includes.label: Local vs global retrofitting techniques
includes.description: Distinction between local retrofitting measures (e.g. member jacketing with FRP) applied when a building has acceptable lateral strength/stiffness, and global retrofitting techniques, both assessed in terms of strengths and weaknesses for seismic upgrading of RC, masonry and steel buildings.

includes.label: Novel seismic retrofitting technologies
includes.description: Development of new technologies for the seismic upgrading of RC, masonry and steel buildings, receiving great attention in academia and engineering practice due to poor structural performance observed in past earthquakes; summarised and assessed for strengths and weaknesses in REEBUILD work.

includes.label: Combined seismic and energy renovation
includes.description: Integrated retrofitting combining seismic strengthening with energy efficiency upgrading of existing buildings, seen as more cost-effective than separate renovations in moderate-to-high seismic regions of Europe; explored via four main intervention types: exoskeletons, interventions on the existing envelope, replacement of the existing envelope, and interventions on horizontal elements. Case studies showed total cost reductions (combining energy, environmental and structural costs) of 42%, 41%, 31% and 47% compared to pre-renovation state.

includes.label: Exoskeleton retrofitting systems
includes.description: One of the four main types of combined renovation interventions identified for integrated seismic and energy upgrading of existing buildings, alongside interventions on the existing envelope, envelope replacement, and interventions on horizontal elements.

includes.label: Building envelope interventions
includes.description: Combined renovation technology category covering interventions on the existing building envelope (and its replacement) as part of integrated seismic and energy renovation solutions, with varying levels of technological maturity from conceptual to experimentally validated.

includes.label: Horizontal element interventions
includes.description: Combined renovation technology category addressing interventions on horizontal structural elements (e.g. floors/slabs) as part of integrated seismic and energy renovation of existing buildings.

includes.label: Life-cycle cost assessment of retrofitting
includes.description: Simplified methodology assessing seismic, energy and environmental performance of a building at three life-cycle stages (initial renovation time, extended lifetime, end-of-life) converting results into equivalent monetary costs, used to compare alternative combined renovation solutions and demonstrate economic benefits across case studies.

includes.label: Regional prioritisation of building renovation
includes.description: Assessment of seismic risk, energy performance and socioeconomic vulnerability at regional level across Europe to identify priority regions and intervention scenarios for integrated building retrofitting, supporting an EU action plan and engagement with national, regional and local authorities.

includes.label: Code gaps for retrofitting with new walls
includes.description: Eurocode 8 – Part 3 fully covers retrofitting with FRP or concrete jackets, but does not address retrofitting of RC frames by adding new infill walls; national guidelines (e.g. Greek KANEPE) only partially address such interventions, highlighting a gap in standardised design provisions for this retrofitting technique.

nodes.label: Land-use planning and risk-informed siting
nodes.description: Land-use planning and zoning measures that reduce exposure to seismic and cascading hazards.

includes.label: Strategic urban planning restrictions
includes.description: Risk reduction measures include strategic urban planning that forbids construction near cliff faces, active faults or on soft soils, alongside seismic retrofitting and enforcement of modern design regulations.

includes.label: Improved land-use practices
includes.description: Post-earthquake investigations contribute to a safer and more resilient built environment, including improved land-use practices that support community resilience, as one of the goals achieved through coordinated post-earthquake investigations.

includes.label: Build Back Better land-use planning
includes.description: Post-disaster reconstruction offers an opportunity to introduce or reform regulatory processes aiming to 'Build Back Better', including implementing land use planning, improving the quality and safety of the built environment, and strengthening community resilience to earthquakes, as learned from past earthquakes such as Kobe and L'Aquila where many damaged buildings lacked earthquake-resistance provisions.

nodes.label: Seismic risk assessment and modelling
nodes.description: Hazard, exposure, vulnerability and risk models and national risk assessments for earthquakes.

includes.label: Fragility and vulnerability functions
includes.description: Ground shaking distribution at asset locations is combined with fragility or vulnerability functions to assess damage or losses respectively.

includes.label: Earthquake loss estimation software
includes.description: Software packages such as ELER, OpenQuake, SELENA, CAPRA and HAZUS are used to perform earthquake scenario and probabilistic loss assessments, incorporating uncertainties from hazard, exposure and vulnerability components.

includes.label: Urban earthquake scenario projects
includes.description: European initiatives such as RISK-EU and LESSLOSS developed earthquake scenarios for large urban centres (e.g. Bucharest, Catania, Nice, Lisbon, Istanbul, Sofia, Thessaloniki) exploring impacts of seismic events.

includes.label: Critical infrastructure seismic stress testing
includes.description: The STREST project explored the impact of specific seismic events on critical facilities such as industrial structures, as part of harmonized stress-test approaches for non-nuclear critical infrastructure.

includes.label: PSHA-based probabilistic seismic risk assessment
includes.description: Classic PSHA-based risk or probabilistic event-based risk analyses are used to assess earthquake losses, considering all possible earthquakes affecting a site with their probabilities of occurrence, producing probabilistic damage and loss estimates with uncertainties.

includes.label: Average annual loss mapping
includes.description: Probabilistic earthquake loss assessment example for Portugal calculated average annual losses at county level using a time-independent PSHA model, informing local governments and civil protection authorities for risk-reduction measures.

includes.label: Risk-informed seismic code calibration
includes.description: Seismic risk assessment outputs are used to improve and enforce seismic codes, calibrate seismic design actions in codes, and establish minimum hazard levels below which seismic zonation is unnecessary, in coordination with Eurocode 8 (CEN/TC250 SC8).

includes.label: Retrofitting campaign planning via risk assessment
includes.description: Risk assessment results support the development of retrofitting campaigns and improved urban planning to reduce seismic risk, as illustrated by Italy's ~EUR 1 billion national seismic prevention programme in 2009.

includes.label: Seismic risk transfer and financing mechanisms
includes.description: Risk assessment supports development of financial mechanisms to transfer seismic risk from the public sector to the international reinsurance market and to strategically allocate funds for risk reduction and prevention.

includes.label: Cascading and systemic risk modelling
includes.description: Modern inter-related systems (building stock, power, water, transportation) mean a seismic event may trigger cascading effects; explored in European projects Syner-G and STREST through multi-hazard, multi-vulnerability analysis.

includes.label: Multidisciplinary risk assessment partnership
includes.description: Earthquake impact assessment incorporates seismology, earthquake engineering and social sciences; neglecting any field reduces accuracy and usefulness of risk metrics; stakeholders from public/private sectors should be involved.

includes.label: EU-funded earthquake risk research knowledge base
includes.description: Two decades of EU-funded projects have advanced earthquake hazard, vulnerability and risk modelling science; leveraging this wealth of resources reduces replication of effort in applying existing knowledge to DRM.

includes.label: Satellite and VGI-based exposure characterisation
includes.description: Satellite imagery and volunteered geographic information (VGI) enable characterisation of the built environment with unprecedented temporal and spatial detail for risk modelling, going beyond building-by-building data collection.

includes.label: Socioeconomic recovery capacity in risk modelling
includes.description: Risk-reduction strategy development should incorporate socioeconomic aspects and the capability of society to recover from destructive events, not only direct physical impact.

includes.label: Building-by-building exposure data collection
includes.description: For local assessment, mobile devices and tools such as GEM's Inventory Data Capture Tool are used to geo-reference and classify buildings according to structural attributes for exposure modelling using a building taxonomy.

includes.label: National/regional census-based exposure modelling
includes.description: For large-scale exposure modelling, building census surveys and socioeconomic data (construction material, storeys, age) are used, with mapping schemes linking census attributes to vulnerability classes.

includes.label: Seismogenic source and ground motion models
includes.description: Seismic hazard models comprise seismogenic source models (spatial/temporal distribution of seismicity via point, area, fault sources) and ground motion models (mean/std of shaking intensity conditional on magnitude, distance, site parameters such as Vs,30), e.g. the European Seismic Hazard Model 2020 (ESHM20).

includes.label: European seismic hazard and risk model repositories
includes.description: EFEHR hosts ESHM20 and ESRM20 model repositories with hazard maps, curves, spectra and input files used in OpenQuake for risk calculations, publicly accessible for European seismic risk assessment.

includes.label: National seismic risk assessment under UCPM
includes.description: Countries participating in the Union Civil Protection Mechanism develop national risk assessments including earthquake hazard; in 2018, more than 20 countries assessed earthquake risk, some considering cross-border and cascading effects such as tsunami, landslides, infrastructure disruption and industrial accidents, following ISO 31000:2018 process.

includes.label: Maximum probable/credible earthquake scenario
includes.description: A hazard scenario approach using the largest earthquake reasonably expected in a region, based on historical events and known geologic faults or source zones, used for deterministic risk assessment.

includes.label: Probabilistic seismic hazard disaggregation
includes.description: Disaggregation analysis determines the most likely earthquake scenario (magnitude-distance pair) governing hazard at a site, conditional on a given ground motion level or return period.

includes.label: Ground-motion prediction and simulation models
includes.description: Ground motion is modelled via empirical ground-motion prediction equations or more sophisticated stochastic simulation methods generating time histories and duration for seismic scenarios, used for nonlinear dynamic analysis, seismic design and retrofitting.

includes.label: Sendai Framework indicator-based risk scenarios
includes.description: Seismic risk scenarios assess Sendai Framework indicators including fatalities, injuries, damaged/destroyed dwellings, direct economic loss relative to GDP, direct economic loss in housing sector, damage to critical infrastructure, and disruption of basic services.

includes.label: Machine learning for seismic risk identification
includes.description: Machine learning and deep learning techniques have been explored for seismic risk identification (hazard and vulnerability), analysis (fragility and damage assessment) and treatment (mitigation via structural control), though not yet mature for national-level implementation.

includes.label: Europe-wide earthquake scenarios initiative
includes.description: A flagship initiative under the 'Anticipate' key area aims to develop Europe-wide earthquake scenarios as part of broader disaster risk management efforts.

includes.label: Real-time earthquake loss and damage assessment systems
includes.description: National systems such as CAPRA (Latin America), READY and SUPREME (Japan) perform rapid, real-time loss and damage evaluation, e.g. liquefaction and road/building damage monitoring, or gas pipeline safety control, using dense strong motion networks.

includes.label: National housing stock earthquake risk assessment
includes.description: National civil protection authorities assess earthquake risk to housing stock combining probabilistic seismic hazard evaluation with detailed damage data from past earthquakes, producing updated seismic risk maps accessible to citizens via web tools, extended to specific building typologies such as schools and churches.

includes.label: Regional seismic hazard distribution mapping
includes.description: Many European countries, particularly in the South-East, are exposed to earthquake hazard consistent with tectonic plate boundaries (Eurasian-African) running through the Mediterranean; seismic hazard and risk is mapped at the site or regional level combining hazard, exposure and vulnerability.

includes.label: Tracking of earthquake losses via EU Solidarity Fund events
includes.description: A record of significant European earthquakes since 2002 for which the EU Solidarity Fund intervened, with damage figures ranging from tens of millions to over EUR 21 billion, used to characterise seismic risk and loss patterns across the region; earthquakes account for 45% of total EU Solidarity Fund aid for natural disasters since 2002.

nodes.label: Structural testing and research
nodes.description: Experimental structural testing, pseudo-dynamic and reaction wall testing supporting seismic engineering research.

includes.label: Pseudo-dynamic testing method
includes.description: On-line computer numerical simulation combined with actual physical measurements of structural properties. Accelerogram input drives a discrete model (limited degrees of freedom, e.g. storey displacements); equations of motion solved with explicit Newmark time integration; horizontal displacements applied by actuators at each storey while measured restoring forces are fed back into the simulation. Does not need to run in real time since inertial/damping forces are modelled numerically. Developed and refined at ELSA since the early 1990s with digital controllers and reliable time-step integration algorithms, enabling reliable tests on multi-storey real-size buildings, bidirectional action, and substructured bridges with realistic-size piers.

sources.doc: seismic retrofitting of rc frames with rc infilling-LBNA26470ENN.pdf

includes.label: Reaction wall testing facility
includes.description: The ELSA Reaction Wall consists of a reinforced concrete vertical wall rigidly connected to a horizontal floor, permitting bi-directional testing of real-size multi-storey buildings and critical elements of larger structures such as bridges. The 16 m-tall, 21 m-long wall has two reaction platforms totalling 760 m2 and is equipped with 28 actuators (capacities 0.2-3.0 MN, strokes ±0.125 to ±0.5 m) controlled by an in-house system enabling step and continuous pseudo-dynamic methods with substructuring.

includes.label: Full-scale building testing
includes.description: Testing of entire real-size multi-storey buildings (rather than scaled specimens or isolated elements) to capture realistic failure modes, higher-mode effects and boundary conditions. Examples include a full-scale two-storey flat slab building (3x2 bays, spans 4.5-5 m), a three-storey precast residential building (15x16 m plan, 10.9 m height, possibly the largest specimen ever tested in a laboratory), and a full-scale steel building mock-up representing the ground floor of a four-storey prototype.

includes.label: Hybrid simulation testing
includes.description: Component-level experimental technique that accounts for interaction between a tested physical specimen and a realistic virtual sub-assembly instantiated in finite element software, avoiding the cost and complexity of testing an entire structure. Used successfully on concrete bridges and steel frames, and applied to a full-scale steel building with passive fire protections where ten seismic tests investigated structural and non-structural component performance.

includes.label: Staged seismic intensity test sequence
includes.description: Testing protocol applying increasing seismic intensity levels tied to limit states: Full Operation (FO, elastic response), Damage Limitation (DL, 95-year return period), Significant Damage (SD, 475-year return period), and Near Collapse (NC, 2475-year return period), consistent with EN 1998-1 and EN 1998-3. Used to progressively assess structural performance from elastic response through moderate damage to extensive damage/near collapse, including replacement of damaged dissipative elements (e.g. links) between stages and pushover tests to increase residual drift.

includes.label: Cyclic loading testing to failure
includes.description: Testing sequence applying repeated cyclic loading beyond seismic pseudo-dynamic tests, up to ultimate drift capacity of the structure, used to characterise post-critical behaviour and failure modes, e.g. of flat slab-column connections after seismic damage, including testing strengthened connections to failure (6% drift ratio).

includes.label: Post-damage strengthening testing
includes.description: Experimental verification of repair/strengthening techniques applied to structural elements damaged during seismic testing, such as using bolted bars in holes drilled through a slab to strengthen damaged slab-column connections, followed by further cyclic testing to assess effectiveness; good performance of strengthened connections observed after 6% drift ratio tests.

includes.label: Transnational access to research infrastructure
includes.description: Programme allowing researchers from across Europe and internationally to access the ELSA Reaction Wall facility within EU framework programmes for research and innovation (FP4 through Horizon Europe), fostering collaboration between laboratories, universities and industry and supporting mobility of researchers.

includes.label: Structural instrumentation for testing
includes.description: Extensive instrumentation deployed during structural tests to capture local and global behaviour, including local and global displacement transducers, inclinometers, strain gages, through-crack sensors, and internal force/moment measurement systems within structural members, enabling detailed characterisation of deformation, damage and failure mechanisms.

includes.label: Aftershock sequence testing
includes.description: Hybrid simulation tests applying a sequence of two identical shocks (main shock and aftershock) to assess variation in seismic response of structural and non-structural elements; results showed similar performance to the main shock except one configuration (firewalls) lost some dissipation capacity (-12%) after the aftershock.

includes.label: Re-centring dissipative system testing
includes.description: Experimental testing of structural concepts combining re-centring capability (via moment resisting frames) with removable dissipative members (bolted links) to overcome the economic losses and downtime associated with conventional dissipative seismic design; tested through a sequence of pseudo-dynamic tests with link replacement between damage stages.

includes.label: Non-structural element seismic testing
includes.description: Testing of the seismic performance of non-structural elements and their interaction with the primary structure, including cladding panel connections on precast buildings and fire protection elements (calcium silicate boards, spray-based fire protection, firewalls) on steel buildings; results fed into design guidelines later adopted as ISO standards.

includes.label: Precast connection testing
includes.description: Pseudo-dynamic testing of precast concrete building arrangements and their connections to evaluate seismic behaviour, demonstrating substantial equivalence in safety to traditional cast-in-situ structures even without monolithic joints; outcomes contributed to guidelines later adopted as an ISO standard.

nodes.label: Early warning and preparedness
nodes.description: Early warning systems, rapid impact estimation, forecasting and preparedness planning before and during events.

includes.label: Earthquake early warning systems
includes.description: Networks of seismic sensors detect initial P-wave pulses and analyse data in real-time to predict expected shaking intensity, sending alerts to surrounding areas with up to several seconds to minutes of lead time. Alerts often target automatic shutdown of critical infrastructure (gas pipelines, trains) rather than the public directly. Effectiveness depends on density and proximity of seismic networks to active faults. Examples include Japan's bullet train system and Mexico City's system; European projects (SAFER, REAKT) studied feasibility but no large-scale operational EU system exists.

includes.label: Tsunami early warning
includes.description: Earthquake parameters (location, depth, magnitude) detected by seismic networks feed Tsunami Early Warning Centres to assess tsunamigenic potential; warnings are pushed to threatened coastal areas, sometimes with hours of lead time to evacuate. For near-coast earthquakes warning may not be possible and strong/long shaking should prompt self-evacuation.

includes.label: Earthquake forecasting
includes.description: Long-term hazard assessments using historical data and short-term aftershock forecasts based on exponential decay patterns can indicate increased risk; earthquakes themselves cannot be predicted.

includes.label: GDACS rapid impact estimation
includes.description: Within about 30 minutes of a main event, GDACS automatically defines an alert level for humanitarian activation, producing an event map, shakemap, meteorological forecast map, exposure estimate (intensity polygons and affected places) and exposed population figures. For the M7.7 Myanmar earthquake, GDACS issued a RED notification 19 minutes after the event (and another 18 minutes after a 6.7M aftershock), sent to more than 40,000 users, with estimates updated as shaking intensity data was refined.

includes.label: Near-real-time loss assessment systems
includes.description: Systems that estimate expected human and economic losses shortly after a seismic event using existing exposure and vulnerability models and computed ground shaking; USGS PAGER is a well-known global system, with national systems also developed for Italy, Bulgaria, Romania, Portugal and Turkey. The EU-funded ARISTOTLE pilot project provides scientific support to the European Emergency Response Coordination Centre for earthquakes and other hazards.

includes.label: Collaborative rapid impact modelling with partners
includes.description: JRC collaborates with Global Earthquake Model (GEM) using OpenQuake to produce impact estimations (fatalities, injuries, building damage, economic damage) shared with ERCC and global humanitarian organisations to identify affected areas, plan satellite acquisitions, guide deployment of international responders and quantify response funding; JRC is integrating GEM impact modelling into GDACS.

includes.label: PAGER earthquake impact scale
includes.description: The USGS Prompt Assessment of Global Earthquakes for Response (PAGER) system uses an Earthquake Impact Scale to provide summary alert levels (PAGER alerts), serving as the primary tool for categorizing earthquake impact and informing activation of post-earthquake investigations.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Pre-event investigation planning
includes.description: Advance planning activities to ensure readiness for post-earthquake investigation activation, including maintaining a contact catalog of partner organizations for coordination calls and a database of regional/State earthquake Technical Clearinghouse plans and key contacts, with processes to quickly launch Clearinghouses where absent.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Earthquake response exercises and drills
includes.description: Exercises should be conducted within 1 year of plan completion and at least every 3 years thereafter to ensure representatives are prepared to launch and support post-earthquake investigations; realistic scenarios vary intensity, geography, stakeholders, and may include cascading hazards (tsunamis, fire-following earthquake). Results are recorded as playbooks; exercises include training on safety, ethics and protocols.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Public awareness and self-protection campaigns
includes.description: Communication and awareness-raising to promote a risk culture, guiding implementation of self-protection measures to take before, during and after an earthquake, such as creating a family plan, preparing an emergency kit, and practicing earthquake drills (e.g. shakeout drills); linked to the EU 'Prepare' goal and the prepareEU programme raising disaster awareness and resilience among citizens.

includes.label: Scenario-based rapid impact assessment tools
includes.description: Research efforts tailor scenario-based rapid impact assessment tools to meet the needs of professionals in emergency planning and response, as well as public education and improving societal resilience.

includes.label: Post-earthquake investigation coordination plan
includes.description: A structured, phased plan (Phase 1: Plan Activation minutes-days; Phase 2: Perishable Data Reconnaissance days-months; Phase 3: Research and Knowledge Transfer months-years) coordinating NEHRP agency post-earthquake investigations to maximize learning and quickly translate lessons into practices that mitigate future earthquake effects, improving societal preparedness and response/recovery.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: National risk assessment framework
includes.description: Under the Union Civil Protection Mechanism, Member States are required to develop risk assessments, assess risk management capability, and refine disaster risk management planning, including cross-border considerations; the EU disaster resilience goals include improving risk assessment, anticipating and planning for DRM, increasing risk awareness and preparedness, improving early warning systems, and enhancing UCPM response capacity; earthquake is one of 16 hazards for disaster scenario development.

nodes.label: Search and rescue operations
nodes.description: Urban search and rescue operations conducted by national or international teams after earthquakes.

includes.label: INSARAG-certified USAR teams
includes.description: Specialized INSARAG-certified urban search and rescue (USAR) teams are crucial for detecting and extracting survivors trapped in collapsed buildings; they are among the first responders deployed, with speed critical for saving lives.

includes.label: Golden rescue window 24-48h
includes.description: 85-95% of persons rescued alive from collapsed buildings are rescued in the first 24-48 hours after an earthquake, though under ideal conditions (food, water, temperate climate) trapped victims may survive considerably longer.

includes.label: Heavy/medium/light USAR team classification
includes.description: International USAR teams are classified and deployed by capability as Heavy USAR (HUSAR), Medium USAR (MUSAR) and Light USAR, plus canine K-9 search and rescue teams; e.g. for Türkiye 6 Heavy, 24 Medium, 1 Light and 1 canine K-9 SAR team were offered via UCPM.

includes.label: International USAR team mobilisation
includes.description: Following a request for international assistance, dozens of countries mobilise and deploy USAR teams through mechanisms such as UCPM and bilaterally; e.g. in Türkiye 31 UCPM USAR teams plus dozens more from other countries were deployed/mobilising within days; in Myanmar 23 USAR teams from 9 countries deployed.

includes.label: USAR operational base identification
includes.description: National authorities identify bases of operations for incoming international USAR teams in the most affected locations; e.g. AFAD identifying bases in Hatay, Kahramanmaraş, Adıyaman and Gaziantep for the 31 accepted UCPM USAR teams.

includes.label: Tracking of persons rescued
includes.description: Number of persons rescued by deployed search and rescue teams is tracked and reported; e.g. 45 people rescued by UCPM-deployed search and rescue teams as of 9 February in Türkiye.

includes.label: National USAR teams
includes.description: National disaster management agencies deploy their own USAR teams and equipment from regional centres in coordination with international teams; e.g. Thailand's DDPM deployed a 77-person USAR team and equipment, working with Bangkok's emergency teams and international USAR teams.

includes.label: Insufficient search and rescue coverage
includes.description: In some contexts search and rescue capacity is insufficient relative to needs; reported that only 5% of needed search and rescue operations were being covered in Syria, with UN aid not meeting needs of affected people.

includes.label: Local/community rescue support
includes.description: Local White Helmets and communities called for international support for rescue operations where international aid was limited, indicating local volunteer rescue efforts in the immediate aftermath before international teams arrive at scale.

includes.label: USAR coordination liaison with UNDAC
includes.description: A dedicated UNDAC USAR Liaison Officer (LO) is appointed to link USAR operations, coordinated via the Urban Search and Rescue Coordination Cell (UCC), with the overall humanitarian operation; international USAR teams and UNDAC exchange information via the GDACS Virtual On-Site Operations Coordination Centre (VOSOCC).

includes.label: USAR operations in adverse weather
includes.description: Search and rescue teams prepare to work in severe weather conditions, such as snow and sub-zero temperatures forecast during the Türkiye earthquake response, which can hinder operations.

includes.label: Search and rescue equipment requests
includes.description: Affected governments request search and rescue teams and equipment as part of international assistance requests; e.g. Syria requested search and rescue teams and equipment, shelter items and medicines through the EU civil protection mechanism.

nodes.label: Relief distribution and shelter
nodes.description: Response operations providing shelter, relief distributions, field hospitals and WASH services.

includes.label: Relief item distribution
includes.description: Distribution of shelter items (tents, blankets, heaters), food rations, bottled water, household items and essential living items to affected populations; market support and cash incentives should be considered. In Türkiye, UCPM in-kind assistance included requests for 50,000 family winter tents, 100,000 blankets and 50,000 heaters, with 6 EU Member States offering over 125,300 items; rescEU mobilised 500 Relief Housing Units, 2,000 tents and 8,000 beds.

includes.label: Field hospitals and emergency medical care
includes.description: Local medical facilities are often overwhelmed by injured individuals; temporary field hospitals equipped with emergency medical personnel, supplies and equipment are essential for treating those in need. In Türkiye/Syria response, Emergency Medical Teams (EMT) and medical teams were deployed via UCPM, including EMT1, EMT2 and medical consumables, devices and medical evacuation transportation.

includes.label: WASH services
includes.description: Water supply, treatment and reconstruction of water supply systems and drainage/sewer systems is vital; without proper sanitation and waste management the situation deteriorates rapidly, increasing risk of communicable diseases. Distribution of hygiene items, latrines and hygiene promotion should be prioritised. In Syria, WASH needs included rehabilitation of water structures, water trucking, garbage removal, hygiene assistance and disease surveillance due to contaminated water disruptions.

includes.label: Psychosocial support
includes.description: Physiological/psychosocial support for affected people is needed; included in Syria's immediate humanitarian needs (mental health services and support) and UNDP's short-term response priorities (0-3 months), as well as mid-term rehabilitation.

includes.label: Reception and Departure Centre for relief teams
includes.description: On arrival, an RDC for international relief teams should be established at the airport to support incoming response capacity; UNDAC team members may stay behind at the airport to support it and liaise with national authorities.

includes.label: Cash-based and market support assistance
includes.description: Market support and cash incentives should be considered for food/water stabilisation; UNDP's short-term priorities include Multi-purpose Cash Assistance, and mid-term interventions include cash for shelter assistance.

nodes.label: Debris clearance and service restoration
nodes.description: Response operations for debris clearance and restoration of lifelines and essential services.

includes.label: Debris removal for access
includes.description: Rubble from collapsed buildings blocks roads and prevents access; heavy construction equipment (bulldozers, excavators, cranes) and crews are indispensable for clearing roadways, providing access to blocked areas and enabling search and rescue. Finding disposal sites for rubble can be a challenge and debris should be recycled where possible. In Türkiye/Syria response, heavy machines, fuel and equipment for debris removal were identified as priority needs, with debris removal for humanitarian access as a short-term (0-3 months) priority and debris removal and waste management for recovery as a mid-term (3-18 months) priority.

includes.label: Power supply restoration
includes.description: Electrical infrastructure can be severely damaged by earthquakes; bringing in generators, repair crews and equipment and coordinating repairs is key to restoring power access. In Türkiye, blackouts occurred in multiple locations and roughly 30 substations suffered varying degrees of damage, requiring restoration efforts.

includes.label: Communication network restoration
includes.description: Damaged communications systems isolate people and prevent coordination; rapid deployment of temporary cell towers, satellite phones, radios and internet connectivity aids rescue coordination, supports situational awareness and reconnects the affected population.

includes.label: Water and sanitation system restoration
includes.description: Water supply, treatment and reconstruction of water supply systems and drainage/sewer systems is described as vital after earthquakes; without proper sanitation and waste management the situation deteriorates rapidly and increases risk of communicable disease.

includes.label: Lifeline restoration and repair activities
includes.description: Post-earthquake investigations document details of post-earthquake restoration and repair activities for lifeline systems, including time to restore basic intended functions and service capabilities, recognising inter-system dependencies and cascading impacts of lifeline damage and disruption.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Gas pipeline rupture repair
includes.description: Natural gas transmission pipelines can rupture at multiple points from earthquake shaking, sometimes causing fires; repair and restoration of gas transmission and distribution lines is needed, as seen with the state-owned BOTAS pipeline in Hatay Province rupturing in two sections roughly 3 km apart after the Türkiye-Syria earthquake.

includes.label: Logistics and transport route restoration
includes.description: Increased air traffic, congested air space, reduced airport capacity and damaged roads/rail lines cause delays affecting air and overland relief transport; supply chains are disrupted and temporary solutions are needed to ferry in aid and allow people to leave impacted zones.

includes.label: Rapid damage assessment for recovery planning
includes.description: Rapid damage assessments (e.g. World Bank initial USD 1.78 billion assessment for Türkiye) estimate the magnitude of disaster and identify priority areas for recovery and reconstruction support, feeding into early recovery and Post Disaster Needs Assessment processes.

includes.label: Rehabilitation of critical infrastructure
includes.description: Mid-term (3-18 months) recovery interventions include rehabilitation of critical basic and social infrastructure and rehabilitation of local markets and small businesses for livelihood recovery, as part of early rehabilitation and reconstruction planning after the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes.

includes.label: Safety interventions on damaged historical structures
includes.description: Response operations included safety interventions such as removing rubble, supporting facades of masonry buildings, supporting arches and supporting a historical bell tower, as well as preventing access to damaged buildings and preserving statues and paintings, documented after the Molise earthquake.

nodes.label: Response coordination mechanisms
nodes.description: Coordination structures such as UNDAC, clusters, reception and departure centres, and liaison with national authorities.

includes.label: UNDAC team deployment
includes.description: UNDAC teams are mobilised and deployed within hours of an event to support on-site coordination of international response; team members must be self-sufficient for 72 hours. UNDAC members have been deployed (e.g. 18 to the Myanmar earthquake, awaiting entry visas) and alerted following government requests for international assistance.

includes.label: Reception and Departure Centre
includes.description: An RDC for incoming international relief teams is established at the main airport soon after the event (e.g. established 6 February 2023 at Adana Sakirpasa Airport by the UNDAC team). UNDAC members may stay at the airport to support it and liaise with national emergency management representatives on arrival.

includes.label: USAR coordination and liaison
includes.description: UNDAC supports on-site coordination of international USAR operations; a dedicated UNDAC USAR Liaison Officer is appointed to link USAR operations with the overall humanitarian response. Multiple national USAR teams are accepted and assigned bases of operations by national authorities (e.g. AFAD identifying Hatay, Kahramanmaras, Adiyaman and Gaziantep as bases for 31 accepted teams).

includes.label: Civil protection mechanism activation
includes.description: A national government requests international assistance, triggering activation of the EU Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), coordinated by the ERCC, which mobilises in-kind assistance, USAR teams, medical teams and EU Civil Protection Teams (EUCPT with ERCC Liaison Officer and Technical Assistance Support Team).

includes.label: INSARAG network alert
includes.description: A government request for international support triggers an alert for deployment of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) network, mobilising international USAR teams.

includes.label: Emergency Response Coordination Centre role
includes.description: The DG ECHO Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) coordinates mobilisation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, including offers and acceptance of in-kind assistance, response teams and transportation means, and deploys Liaison Officers and Technical Assistance Support Teams to the field.

includes.label: Emergency Medical Team coordination cell
includes.description: A national EMT Coordination Cell is established in-country (e.g. with physical presence in Adana) to coordinate deployed Emergency Medical Teams of various levels (EMT1, EMT2) offered by multiple countries.

includes.label: Joint UNEP/OCHA Environment Unit support
includes.description: The UNEP/OCHA Joint Environmental Unit (JEU) is requested to provide environmental experts (e.g. a dam stability expert) to be associated with the UNDAC team, and can activate the UCPM for environmental expertise.

includes.label: Unified Coordination Group
includes.description: A Unified Coordination Group composed of senior state, tribal, territorial and federal officials (and in certain circumstances local jurisdictions, private sector and NGOs) leads unified coordination staff, organised per Incident Command System principles, from a Joint Field Office, integrating response and recovery efforts of government, private sector and NGOs.

includes.label: National Disaster Recovery Framework

includes.description: A scientific/technical program representative embedded in the federal incident command center is recommended to help incident command personnel interpret and incorporate real-time scientific information (e.g. safety-related) into response and recovery operations, ensuring two-way coordination between scientific investigations and formal emergency management.

includes.label: Pre-event coordination agreements
includes.description: Pre-event engagement, coordination and planning among governmental and nongovernmental partners (geological surveys, emergency management departments, universities, engineering and geoscience organisations, private companies) is identified as crucial for effective earthquake response, formalised through contact lists, informal relationships and exercises such as tabletop exercises.

includes.label: Multilateral and donor funding coordination
includes.description: International financial institutions and the EU mobilise emergency humanitarian and recovery funding in coordination with the response (e.g. EUR 5.2 million EU humanitarian funding, USD 1.78 billion World Bank initial recovery funding, EU and UN emergency aid allocations for Myanmar) alongside appeals by IFRC and WHO.

includes.label: Copernicus emergency mapping activation
includes.description: The Copernicus Emergency Mapping Service (satellite mapping) is activated by the ERCC to support damage assessment, with JRC providing technical support; used for multiple areas of interest to estimate affected buildings and roads, feeding into coordinated response and recovery planning.

includes.label: Liaison with national authorities
includes.description: Arriving international teams liaise with National Emergency Management representatives at the airport or shortly after arrival, and alert the Resident/Humanitarian Coordinator of their arrival, ensuring coordination between international responders and host-nation authorities.

includes.description: Centralized, publicly available web page disseminating information on ongoing investigations, preliminary findings and funding opportunities, with links to reconnaissance field reports, data, workshops and conference proceedings, intended for researchers, policymakers and the public.

includes.label: International researcher partnerships
includes.description: International researchers are encouraged to partner with domestic researchers and engage in Technical Clearinghouse coordination after significant earthquakes, increasing resources, enabling joint data collection/sharing/publishing and fostering consistent messaging; formal agreements between agencies may be developed.

includes.label: Perishable data reconnaissance
includes.description: Phase 2 of post-earthquake investigation extending from days to months, focused on gathering, sharing and publishing perishable (fragile, short-lived) data on earthquake effects. Involves coordination among organizations and field teams, with both discipline-specific and interdisciplinary field teams; investigators are expected to follow safe and ethical guidelines (e.g. IRB procedures, ethics training).

includes.label: Data-gathering principles
includes.description: Overarching principles for post-earthquake data collection: investigations should not interfere with emergency response; data should support understanding impacts across all dimensions; observations (photographs, damage surveys, interviews) should be timestamped and geotagged; data shared quickly through the clearinghouse; advanced methods used when appropriate; data collected anticipating preservation in a repository.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Advanced data-collection technologies
includes.description: Use of lidar, drone images, seismic sensors and stations and other advanced data-collection methods in field reconnaissance, with equipment available through shared-use entities such as the NHERI Natural Hazards Reconnaissance Facility, SAGE and GAGE.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Geoscience field data collection
includes.description: Field investigation of seismic sources, aftershocks and documentation of fragile/perishable primary and secondary earthquake effects, including mapping of ground rupture, deformation and ground failures (including areas where failure did not occur); seismic/geodetic data capture mainshock, foreshock, aftershock sequences and ground motions; mapping of gravitational failures, liquefaction areas, and tsunami inundation limits. Involves USGS, academic researchers, NIST, NOAA and NASA.

Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Engineering damage data collection
includes.description: Collection of engineering data immediately after an earthquake, observing and documenting both detected damage and lack thereof in geotechnical systems, buildings and lifelines, to advance empirical methodologies and improve engineering codes, standards and guidelines.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Geotechnical reconnaissance
includes.description: Field data gathering on subsurface soils/rocks and geotechnical systems after seismic events, coordinated (e.g. by GEER-type associations) with geoscience and structural engineering researchers; documents observed failures, geotechnical effects, soil-structure interaction, relationships between geotechnical performance and building/lifeline performance, and cases of resilience.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Documentation of lifeline resilience improvements
includes.description: Documentation of post-earthquake improvements undertaken to allow infrastructure systems and community resilience to surpass pre-earthquake conditions.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Social science field investigations
includes.description: Post-earthquake research on human behavior, decision making, policy and socioeconomic relationships connected to the built and natural environment, using surveys, interviews, observations and secondary data analysis; topics include delivery of early warning messages, human behavior during shaking, emergency response communication, injury/death rates, experiences of marginalized populations, effects of school/business closures, and displacement rates.

includes.label: After-action report
includes.description: A brief report led by coordinating agencies describing how the investigation coordination plan was implemented, what worked well, what could be improved, and recommended changes to the plan.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Reconnaissance dissemination conferences
includes.description: Conferences or events, from about 6 months to 5 years after an earthquake, focused on disseminating reconnaissance findings and lessons learned to technical experts, policymakers and other stakeholders, potentially virtual/hybrid and leveraging existing conferences or earthquake milestones.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Integrative synthesis publication
includes.description: In-depth synthesis report(s), produced within 2 to 5 years after a significant earthquake, bringing together reconnaissance and detailed study findings, with an extensive bibliography, covering damage, disruption and cases of good building performance, distilling lessons for future research, practice and loss-reduction policy.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Sector-specific agency reconnaissance
includes.description: Non-coordinating federal agencies conduct their own post-earthquake reconnaissance focused on their sector mandates (e.g. highway infrastructure reconnaissance by transportation agencies), complementing the main coordinated investigation.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Alignment of reconnaissance with response/recovery frameworks
includes.description: Coordination of post-earthquake reconnaissance data gathering, analysis, curation, publishing and archiving to align with and facilitate national disaster response and recovery frameworks and unified coordination structures.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: Structural assessment field mission
includes.description: Field missions by earthquake engineering laboratory staff to affected areas to carry out on-site assessment of earthquake effects on different categories of structures (masonry buildings, reinforced concrete buildings, churches, bridges and viaducts), informing subsequent earthquake engineering studies; includes collecting photographic documentation and exchanging information with international experts on site.

includes.label: Field mission report production
includes.description: Production of a field mission report giving a thorough overview of significant aspects of an earthquake event, covering the seismological framework, human environment, damage distribution and typology, emergency management data (homeless, casualties, inspected structures) and conclusions drawn from the mission.

includes.label: Site visits with local civil protection and institutions
includes.description: Field mission site visits including university campuses, local civil protection headquarters and heavily damaged 'red zones', with local experts and civil protection officials presenting earthquake effects and emergency management issues to the visiting mission team, sometimes requiring accompaniment by fire brigade for access.

nodes.label: Rapid scientific analysis and mapping
nodes.description: Rapid scientific analyses, satellite mapping and impact estimation products produced soon after an earthquake.

includes.label: Geotechnical data collection
includes.description: Collection and coordination of geotechnical earthquake engineering data after seismic events (e.g. by GEER Association with EERI, NIST, USGS) to document observed failures, geotechnical effects, soil-structure interaction and resilience cases, advancing empirical methods and codes.

sources.doc: Plan To Coordinate Post-Earthqu - Chris Poland.pdf

includes.label: JRC rapid scientific analysis report
includes.description: Successive JRC scientific analysis updates produced within hours to weeks of an earthquake, synthesising hazard, impact, satellite mapping, and response information to support EU policymaking and the ERCC (e.g. multiple updates for the Türkiye-Syria and Myanmar earthquakes).

includes.label: Copernicus EMS rapid mapping activation
includes.description: Activation of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service Rapid Mapping by the ERCC within hours of an earthquake (e.g. 4:43 UTC, less than 4 hours after the M7.8 Türkiye quake; 9:40 a.m. same day for Myanmar following a GDACS alert) to acquire very high resolution optical satellite imagery over areas of interest near epicentres and produce damage assessment maps, with the JRC Copernicus Mapping Team providing technical support.

includes.label: Satellite-based building and road damage assessment
includes.description: Analysis of very high resolution optical (and SAR) satellite imagery to identify damaged/destroyed/possibly damaged building blocks, individual buildings and affected road lengths; results progressively consolidated over days as cloud-free imagery becomes available (e.g. from 488 building blocks/13.2 km roads on day 2 to 4,042 building blocks/72 km roads by day 4, later 1,161 building blocks/3,361 buildings/84 km roads with AOI-level breakdowns), also identifying temporary/spontaneous camps.

includes.label: Population exposure estimation from satellite AOIs
includes.description: Estimation of the population living within satellite-mapped areas of interest around earthquake epicentres using population density grids (e.g. based on census data adjusted to UN World Population Prospects), used to characterise exposed population per AOI (ranging from about 3.95 to 4.28 million people across updates).

includes.label: GDACS rapid impact estimation and alert
includes.description: Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (GDACS, JRC/EC-ECHO managed) issues red/qualitative alert notifications and casualty/impact estimates minutes after an earthquake using USGS shakemaps (e.g. RED notification 19 minutes after the M7.7 Myanmar earthquake, sent to over 40,000 users), with estimates refined over following days as shaking intensity data improves.

includes.label: Near-real-time earthquake loss estimation systems
includes.description: Open-source and operational software tools (e.g. PAGER, QLARM, Hazus-MH, SELENA, OpenQuake, ARCH DSS, IRMA, RASOR, CAPRA, Rapid-N) that provide rapid post-event evaluations of damage, casualties and economic losses based on earthquake magnitude, location and shake/ground-motion maps, typically producing early impact assessments within 5-15 minutes to 24 hours; comparisons with real events show economic loss magnitude generally well predicted but casualties often overestimated.

includes.label: Rapid dam breach simulation
includes.description: Preliminary dam discharge/dam break calculations performed rapidly after an earthquake to anticipate downstream flood impact under a worst-case total breach scenario, including arrival time to populated areas and flow depths (e.g. Maydanki Dam scenario reaching Afrin after 1h45, flow depths ~2.7 m; Sultansuyu Dam scenario; Sedawgyi Dam scenario estimating up to 100,000 people potentially affected in case of total breach).

includes.label: ECHO daily flash and situational maps
includes.description: Daily co-produced JRC-ERCC situational products (ECHO Daily Flash and ECHO Daily Maps) updating humanitarian impact and international response information across affected countries in the days following an earthquake (e.g. four Flash reports and two Daily Maps produced in the first days after the Myanmar earthquake).

includes.label: Multi-stakeholder scientific analyst coordination
includes.description: Daily coordination among the global community of disaster analysts and key scientific partners (Global Earthquake Model Foundation, WMO, UNOCHA-coordinated Assessment & Analysis Cell) to share earthquake impact estimations and expertise with operational decision-makers (ERCC, UNOCHA, humanitarian community).

includes.label: Conflict-affected damage interpretation caveat
includes.description: Caution needed when interpreting satellite-based damage assessments in conflict zones, as buildings may have been damaged/destroyed by prior airstrikes and villages may have been depopulated before the earthquake, confounding attribution of damage to the seismic event.

includes.description: Reconstruction of water supply, treatment and drainage/sewer systems is vital after an earthquake; without it, survivor conditions deteriorate rapidly and communicable disease risk rises.

includes.label: Post Disaster Needs Assessment
includes.description: Longer-term assessments organized by European Commission services and UN development agencies, led by national authorities, to quantify needs and advocate with donors for early rehabilitation and reconstruction; notably longer in timing than preliminary rapid assessments.

includes.description: A donors' conference called by the European Commission President and the Council to raise funds for early rehabilitation and reconstruction after a major earthquake.

includes.description: International financial institutions (e.g., World Bank) announce initial funding for a country's recovery and reconstruction efforts and commence rapid damage assessments to estimate disaster magnitude and identify priority areas for recovery and reconstruction support.

includes.label: Mid-term recovery interventions (3-18 months)
includes.description: Mid-term response interventions focusing on in-depth post disaster impact assessment, debris removal and waste management for recovery, rehabilitation of critical basic and social infrastructure, rehabilitation of local markets and small businesses for livelihood recovery, and cash-for-shelter assistance.

includes.label: Rehabilitation of critical and social infrastructure
includes.description: Mid-term recovery priority of rehabilitating critical basic and social infrastructure damaged by the earthquake.

includes.label: Rehabilitation of local markets and livelihoods
includes.description: Recovery interventions aimed at rehabilitating local markets and small businesses to support livelihood recovery for affected populations.

includes.label: Cash-for-shelter assistance
includes.description: Mid-term recovery intervention providing cash assistance for shelter as part of early rehabilitation and reconstruction response.

includes.label: Build Back Better reconstruction
includes.description: Post-disaster reconstruction offers an opportunity to introduce or reform regulatory processes, implement land-use planning, improve quality and safety of the built environment, strengthen community resilience and capitalise on long-term earthquake risk reduction efforts, as seen after major earthquakes where most damaged buildings lacked adequate seismic provisions.

includes.label: Combined seismic and energy renovation financing instruments
includes.description: Legislation, strategies and financing instruments (e.g., tax deductions, green bonds, loans, national programmes in Bulgaria, Italy, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia) used to upgrade building stock by combining seismic safety with energy renovation, recognised in national recovery and resilience plans and long-term renovation strategies of several EU countries.

includes.label: Reconstruction-driven material shortages and environmental impacts
includes.description: Increased demand for construction materials in a very short time after a major earthquake can lead to shortages of natural building materials and subsequent environmental impacts such as coastal erosion, saline intrusion and illegal mining.

includes.label: Demolition of damaged buildings and traffic congestion
includes.description: After a major earthquake, demolition of damaged buildings and the associated traffic congestion are challenges faced during the reconstruction phase.

includes.label: EU Solidarity Fund support for recovery
includes.description: The European Union Solidarity Fund has intervened to provide financial aid after significant earthquakes in Europe causing losses of billions of euros; earthquakes account for 45% of total aid approved by the Fund for natural disasters since 2002.

nodes.description: Documentation and transfer of lessons learned from past earthquakes into codes, research and training.

includes.label: Domestic vs international lesson transfer
includes.description: Domestic earthquakes offer the best opportunity to evaluate seismic hazards and directly implement lessons in national codes and practices, while international earthquakes, especially in countries with similar codes/geology, also provide valuable learning opportunities for improving national (e.g. U.S.) codes and practices, though international investigations face added challenges such as need for local collaboration, language proficiency and restricted travel.

includes.label: Field observations informing codes and plans

nodes.description: National and local government bodies, civil protection and emergency management agencies.

includes.label: Local emergency operations centers (COM/COC)
includes.description: Mixed Operative Centres (C.O.M.) and Municipal Operative Centres (C.O.C.) were established in the most important towns of the affected area immediately after the Molise earthquakes to manage the emergency, headed by mayors at municipal level and coordinating assistance to local authorities, damage estimation, administrative support, transport and road management, public safety, monument preservation, information, urgent technical services, scientific research, public health, evacuation, logistics, volunteer coordination and telecommunications.

includes.label: National disaster management coordination
includes.description: National authorities (e.g., Government of Türkiye, Syrian government) coordinate the government-led emergency response, request international assistance, and work with agencies such as the Turkish Red Crescent supporting disaster management, social services, nutrition and migration response across several sectors.

includes.label: Formal request for international assistance
includes.description: Following the earthquake, the Republic of Türkiye and later the Syrian government formally requested international assistance (search and rescue teams, equipment, shelter items, medicines) through mechanisms such as the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, triggering mobilization of EUCPM and activation of UNDAC by UN OCHA.

includes.label: State/local/tribal emergency management agencies
includes.description: State, local (county and city) and Tribal emergency management departments, along with geological surveys, transportation agencies, building departments, public works and utility departments, play key roles in post-earthquake investigations and response, often holding primary roles in technical clearinghouses and regional expertise.

includes.label: Federal agency coordination in response
includes.description: NEHRP federal agencies (FEMA, NIST, NSF, USGS) and non-NEHRP federal agencies (e.g., FHWA, NOAA, NASA, EPA, CDC, HUD, DOT, USACE) coordinate post-earthquake investigations and provide capabilities such as transportation, energy, environmental, health, housing and remote sensing assessments, supporting state and local response.

includes.label: National Response Framework activation
includes.description: The U.S. National Response Framework (NRF), based on the Incident Command System and National Incident Management System, identifies key roles, responsibilities and coordinating structures (15 Emergency Support Functions) across government levels for immediate response following an earthquake, coordinated with the National Disaster Recovery Framework for initial recovery.

includes.label: FEMA mitigation and preparedness grant programs
includes.description: FEMA operates grant and assistance programs enabling states to develop mitigation, preparedness and response plans, purchase instrumentation, inventory and conduct seismic safety inspections of critical structures and lifelines, update building, land-use and zoning codes, and increase earthquake awareness and education.

includes.label: National seismic risk assessment practice
includes.description: Countries participating in the Union Civil Protection Mechanism develop and regularly update national risk assessments including earthquake hazard; 19 countries included earthquake in their 2015 risk assessment and four more in 2018, reflecting a national-authority-driven practice of risk mitigation and disaster prevention planning.

includes.label: National command center for disaster prevention and mitigation
includes.description: National authorities maintain dedicated command centers for disaster prevention and mitigation (e.g., Department of Meteorology and Hydrology, National Command Center for Disaster Prevention and Mitigation) that coordinate monitoring and response activities during a major earthquake event.
